h: 5. Toolkit is one playbook for every tool
6. A workspace is shared or private as a whole
x: Slate is one home for every AI coding tool: every session live on your Mac, and one memory plus one set of skills and rules for all 16 tools. Six ideas underlie it. 1. Everything is a doc # The doc is Slate's universal unit. A group, a project, a design doc and a captured AI session are all rows in one doc table, told apart by an optional doc_type . Docs nest in a tree ( parent_id ), order by a fractional position so drag-reorder never renumbers the tree, and hold their content as block-editor JSON. The same few operations (create, read, update, move, Trash) work everywhere, by hand or by AI. 2. Typed documents give work structure # A doc can be typed : group , project , branch , plan , design , review , meeting , test-plan , bug-report , mission or plain general . The type pre-fills a template and limits where the doc can live. A branch sits under a project . A project sits under a group or stands alone. Knowledge docs (plans, designs, reviews) hang off any of them, so memory tools resolve "the plan for the branch I'm on" without an id. 3. One memory, shared over MCP # Slate is also a memory server . It speaks MCP , so any of the 16 tools , or Slate's own Home , calls the same two verbs: recall at the start of a task loads the relevant context: the brief for your branch, project conventions, project memories. remember at the end saves a decision, result or preference, filed on the doc the hierarchy resolves to. A filesystem watcher captures the sessions themselves, so memory grows even when a tool forgets to write. 4. Agents drive your CLIs # Slate ships no model and asks for no API key. An agent is a thin driver over a CLI you already installed and signed in to: Claude Code , Codex , Cursor , GitHub Copilot , Antigravity , OpenCode , Gemini , Cline , Grok Build , Kiro , Qwen Code , Droid , Hermes Agent , Goose , Kilo Code or Auggie . Slate launches it from Rust, so credentials stay in those tools. A light model works because code resolves the tool and prefills its arguments and the model fills only the gaps. 5. Toolkit is one playbook for every tool # Toolkit is where you write instructions and skills once, in AGENTS.md and .slate/ , and project them into every agent's native config. Change the playbook, run yarn studio sync , and every tool picks it up. Features by Agent says which tools it reaches today. 6. A workspace is shared or private as a whole # Workspaces share by container . A team's workspace is the team's, and everything in it is shared. Your Personal workspace starts unshared and syncs only if you switch its sharing on. Each shared workspace is its own SQLite file; switch from the top of the rail. Nothing is marked doc by doc: private work stays in an unshared workspace. Sharing is one-way, and each doc has one writer, its author. That keeps merge conflicts and version columns out of the design. A teammate's doc opens read-only in the real editor, with a line saying why.

h: If you already removed the app
x: One command removes Slate and puts back what it changed: Copy curl -fsSL https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/uninstall.sh | bash Your workspace is kept. Removing it takes a second, explicit flag. See it first # --dry-run prints every step, lists the accounts it would clean, and changes nothing: Copy curl -fsSL https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/uninstall.sh | bash -s -- --dry-run Check the line that names your workspace and its size. What it removes # Slate's entries in your agents The plugin trees, the capture hooks and the MCP registrations, in exactly the accounts Slate wrote to /Applications/Slate.app The app itself The start-at-login item Slate's entry in System Settings → Login Items, and the ~/Library/LaunchAgents/Slate.plist older versions wrote Logs, cache and webview state Three rebuildable directories under ~/Library Slate installs itself into up to eighteen other products (the 16 agents, Claude Desktop and VS Code). Dragging Slate to the Trash leaves every entry behind, pointing at an app that is gone. So the app undoes its own work first, from a record of the accounts it wrote to. An MCP server you registered yourself is never touched , and neither is a plugin marketplace that only shares a name. What it keeps # Your data folder, ~/Library/Application Support/app.slate.workspace/ : workspace.db , your Personal docs and memory one file for each shared workspace machine.db (settings that describe this computer, the telemetry id and your choices about it) your cloud sign-in file the backups It is plain SQLite, and reinstalling picks the same file up. Slate also leaves what Toolkit wrote into your own project folders (skill folders, instruction files): those belong to the project. Removing the workspace too # Copy curl -fsSL https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/uninstall.sh | bash -s -- --delete-workspace This cannot be undone. It removes the whole data folder; no other copy exists, locally or in the cloud. A shared workspace keeps the rows you published, for its members, until you withdraw them ( Stop sharing ) or remove them with Erase my work . Do that first, and export what you want to keep (Settings → Workspaces → the workspace → Storage). A Personal workspace you moved elsewhere stays where you put it. Options # Flag What it does --dry-run Print every step and change nothing --delete-workspace Also remove the whole data folder: workspaces, machine.db , sign-in file and backups --keep-connections Leave Slate's entries in your agents alone --prefix ‹dir› Look for Slate.app somewhere other than /Applications The script never asks a question, so the destructive half is a flag you type. It removes only Slate. The script reads the bundle id of Slate.app first. If the id is not app.slate.workspace , or cannot be read, the app may be another product with the same name. The script then stops and removes nothing. If you already removed the app # The script still cleans the logs, cache and webview state, and reports that it could not remove the agent entries. They are inert. To remove them, reinstall Slate and run the uninstaller again. Doing it by hand # Copy # 1. Quit Slate, so the running copy cannot write back what the next step removes. osascript -e 'tell application "Slate" to quit' # 2. The agent entries — this is the step that needs the app. /Applications/Slate.app/Contents/MacOS/slate --list-connections # see them /Applications/Slate.app/Contents/MacOS/slate --disconnect-all # remove them # 3. The start-at-login item: the one macOS holds for the app, then the file versions # before 0.1.69 wrote. The launchctl line may print an error when it is not loaded; fine. /Applications/Slate.app/Contents/MacOS/slate --remove-login-item launchctl bootout "gui/$(id -u)/Slate" rm -f ~/Library/LaunchAgents/Slate.plist # 4. The app, and the three rebuildable directories. rm -rf /Applications/Slate.app rm -rf ~/Library/Logs/app.slate.workspace rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/app.slate.workspace rm -rf ~/Library/WebKit/app.slate.workspace # 5. Your workspace — only if you mean it. rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/app.slate.workspace See also # Getting Started Platform & Availability Your Data & Export : get your docs out before you go Connect : what Slate writes into your agents, and when

h: Narrowing to a workspace or a project
x: The Sessions tab lists every AI-CLI session on this machine, live, for the 16 agents. It shows who is working, who needs you and where each runs. Nothing to install: any tool whose transcripts the capture watcher sees (non-default config directories too) is tracked. Claude Code lists its own sessions ( claude agents --json ), so its rows carry the real session id, the process and whether a background job finished. Other tools are read from transcripts and the process table. Measured on Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, Gemini, Hermes Agent and Goose; unverified on the rest ( Features by Agent ). A row shows the session's name when it has one. Sub-agents are not sessions. The parent's row counts the live ones and expands to name them; on the map each is a pip around its session. Only recently active ones show, and none can be stopped (they run in the parent's process). What you see # The list shows live sessions on the whole computer. An ended session folds into Just finished and Earlier today . Each live session has one state: State Meaning Needs you The tool finished a turn and is blocked on you. ⌘⇧J goes to the one waiting longest, then the next. The tab header shows the count. Kinds: Needs permission (a tool call waits for your yes), Asks you (the turn ends on a question), Finished (the turn is a report) Working The session wrote a turn in the last 45 seconds. For Claude Code only a turn counts: the bookkeeping lines it adds to a transcript afterwards do not Idle Quiet, and you spoke last. A session that only waits is idle too, however fresh its transcript: its newest step is a running sleep , a shell loop that sleeps until something is ready, or a scheduled wakeup. The wait must be the whole command: sleep 30 && npm test is work. A Claude Code background job that finished but still runs its process is idle too, until Stop ends it (Claude Code keeps that process until claude stop ). Grey dot, no pulse, flow word Waiting When a session starts waiting on a permission or question and Slate is not in front, macOS shows one notification with the question, once per wait (never for waits already there when Slate opened). A finished turn posts nothing; it waits on Home . Tell me when a session needs me in Automations › Built-in turns it off. See How status works . In the menu bar # A Sessions icon shows a count while a session needs you. Its panel lists sessions working or waiting on you, waiting first in Home's order (permission, question, finished), each with kind and tool, and its workspace (a small dot and the name) when they span more than one workspace. Click one to open it. The panel also has Keep the computer awake , New session , Open Slate and Quit Slate . Closing the window only hides it; ⌘Q quits. A hidden window stops reading sessions and all timers and catches up on opening; the count, notification and keep-awake come from the server and keep working. A visible but unused window shows changes within 5 seconds, other timers at a quarter pace. Automations › Built-in has Show Slate in the menu bar (on) and Start Slate at login (off until you choose; it starts with no window, Starting at login ). Narrowing to a workspace or a project # The workspace picker under the side panel's title starts on All workspaces each time the tab opens. Pick one to keep only its sessions, in list and map. A session no workspace claims counts as Personal's. A project picker then appears ( All projects ); a project keeps sessions in it or in its git repositories and branches. Changing the workspace drops the project. The choice lasts while the window is open. Just finished and Earlier today follow both. Opening one of their docs, or All past sessions , from another workspace switches the window to it first. The map and the list # The map shows the machine as a radial tree, group → project → branch → session , in Slate's own greens, not a workspace's colour. The rail reads it out: a row per session with status dot, title, live line and meta line. Hovering one lights the other. Click a row to open the session in a temporary tab; double-click keeps it. Map, row, menu, parking and past sessions: The map and the list . With nothing selected, the main area shows the map. A session's pull request # Slate reads refs/pull/* on origin, asking once a minute, and shows #118 on the row once one points at the branch's tip. The trunk never shows one. The number may belong to a merged or closed pull request (refs cannot tell); a branch sharing its tip with another on origin shows none. Slate opens no pull requests: push and open one on the code host. The keyboard # Tab reaches the rail's rows (cloud rows included); Enter opens one. ↑/↓ or j / k move, Home and End jump to the ends (no wrap), Escape returns focus to the terminal; ↑ or k from outside enters at the last row. On the focused row f starts a second agent in its folder and s stops it (second press within four seconds); on a cloud row both do nothing, and f does nothing on a row with no folder. These letters act only with focus inside the rail and never in a text field; modified chords (⌘⇧J, ⌘K) pass through. From anywhere, ⌘K → Focus the sessions list focuses the first row (listed only while a row is on screen). All keys: Keyboard shortcuts . Stopping a session # Each row whose session can end has an End button. The first click arms it: it turns red and reads End? ( Click End? or press s again to end it ), and stays shown while armed; the second click, or s , ends it. Mouse and keyboard share one arm, which resets after four seconds. Session Stop does Backgrounded Claude claude stop ‹handle› : keeps the conversation , so you can attach again Everything else SIGTERM , so the CLI closes its own MCP subprocesses; the conversation ends A signal is refused when the process is no longer the reported tool (pids are recycled). It works on sessions Slate never started, such as a forgotten CLI in a distant terminal. Quitting Slate ends the sessions it hosts. First,

The Sessions tab draws one list twice, as a radial map and a rail. Use this guide to read a node, row or colour. The map # A radial tree with this machine at the centre: group → project → branch → session . A project on its own sits on the first ring; one in a group, a ring out. A session with no project and no branch hangs from No project . With work in several workspaces, a workspace ring sits inside the group ring. Details and changes are in the window's panel. One button above it says what continuing would do; nothing on that screen types into your terminal. Session Offer Already a background job (Claude Code job, Cursor persist ) No button. h: A worktree made for a session ends with it
x: A worktree is a second checkout of a project on its own branch, so an agent works without touching your main folder. Use New worktree on a project or in the New session tree; a session then starts inside it. The form # Fields: Branch , From (local branches only, nothing fetched) and the Folder it will make, always a sibling of the project. Carry over makes the folder usable: git worktree add copies tracked files only, so a fresh worktree lacks dependencies, .env and build output. The form offers what the project ignores at top level as chips; tick node_modules , skip .DS_Store . Mac: each folder is cloned copy-on-write (no disk cost until a file changes; changes never reach the original). Elsewhere: hard links. Nothing carried is tracked. A missing ticked path or failed copy: the worktree is made, the form names the path, holds the start and offers Start anyway . Setting Meaning Then run One command in the new folder once files are there (build, codegen, submodule fetch). Empty is normal On remove One command in the folder just before the worktree is removed, however it is removed: stop a dev server, drop a local database, free a port. If it fails the worktree stays and the error shows its output (up to 60 seconds) Shell /bin/sh -c on macOS and Linux, with your login shell's PATH and environment; PowerShell on Windows ( cmd if missing); untranslated, so write for your shell Carry over , Then run , On remove and Run preview are saved on the project (so on its group for later worktrees) only when you press Create and start . Closing the form or Back saves nothing. A failed worktree is rolled back. If carry-over or Then run fails, the folder, git's record and the port are removed and the error shows with the command's output. The branch goes too if Slate made it for this worktree and nothing moved it since; an existing branch stays. Fix the cause and press Create and start again with the same name. Ports and temp folders # Each worktree Slate makes gets a free port from 4100 to 4999, kept until removal and stored on this computer only. It is SLATE_PORT in Then run , On remove and every session terminal in or under that folder, so two worktrees can each run vite --port $SLATE_PORT . The row shows :4101 . A hand-made worktree has none. Sessions there also get a temp folder outside the worktree ( TMPDIR , TMP , TEMP ), removed with it. Run preview # Run preview is the command that starts a checkout's dev server, such as yarn dev , offered in a session row's ⋯ . Its terminal opens beside the session, so a failure says why. When the server prints a local address ( http://localhost:5173 ), it opens as a Preview tab in the strip. The preview can reload, open in your browser, or Stop , which ends the server's terminal and closes the tab (the tab also closes when the terminal ends). The first run on a project with no command asks for it; Save and run stores it. A checkout with no project runs it once and saves nothing. Pick (crosshair) turns the preview into a picker. Point at anything to outline it, click, and its description is pasted at the prompt of the session in that folder: the doc it is on, a CSS selector, size and position, deciding styles, its HTML. Nothing is submitted; add the change and press Enter. No screenshot (other origin). The web page is framed through a small proxy on Slate's loopback port that adds one script and serves only a local dev server; hot reload works. Slate keeps proxies for the 16 most recently used dev servers; an older one is closed and starts again when you pick there again. Click the crosshair again for the plain preview. A worktree made for a session ends with it # When the session started in a new worktree ends (you exit the tool or press Stop; closing its tab is not an end), the worktree is removed: State Result Nothing uncommitted, branch merged or empty Folder and branch go Commits not merged Folder goes, branch stays Uncommitted changes Asks once: Keep worktree or Delete forever First, what the session left running there is stopped: every process Slate started for that worktree whose working folder is still inside it (dev server, watcher, test run) gets a polite stop, then a forced one after 3 seconds. Slate knows its own by a mark it gives each session, setup and teardown line for that worktree, never by name or port. A process you started elsewhere is never touched, and shells, multiplexers ( tmux , screen , zellij ), editors and apps are spared even when Slate started them. macOS hides the environment of its own system programs, so one of those ( tail , ruby ) is left running. Windows cannot see another process's folder, so it stops processes whose command line names a path inside the worktree or that listen on its port. A message at the window's bottom says what was returned, Cleaned up · stopped :3000 · 11.2 GB freed , and what happened to worktree and branch. It waits while another session still works in the folder. It never touches a worktree not made for a session: hand-made, another tool's, or one whose session was running when Slate quit. The folder is renamed aside at once and removed in the background. Removing a worktree by hand is under the trash icon on a branch row in New session . It stops no processes and counts nothing. It refuses a checkout with uncommitted work unless you choose to discard it, and can remove the branch too. A dirty branch is marked before the click; a worktree whose folder is gone says missing , and one git did not answer for says not read , never clean. Reviewing and merging a finished branch: Review the branch .

A cloud session runs on your agent's computer. A phone session runs here and you continue it in your tool's app. Both start from New session . Cloud sessions # Claude Code and Codex have them. Gemini and OpenCode have none; Cursor's cloud agents have a web API only ( agent features ). Open New session → Cloud . Write the task, pick a project (git repositories only: the cloud works on a copy). Press Start in cloud . The form says what leaves your computer: Claude clones the project's GitHub remote at its current branch, so push first. With no GitHub remote it uploads the history and uncommitted changes to tracked files (not untracked). Type its name; earlier names are offered and the last one used per project is prefilled. It runs under the project's profile. A Codex row says working, ready, applied or failed (Codex's list is asked once a minute while Sessions is open). Claude keeps no list; its row says the status is on claude.ai. Its doc shows what you asked and every message sent, with the tool's controls: Tool Controls Claude Send a follow-up (Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line; queued, answered on claude.ai). Bring back opens it in a new worktree with the whole conversation, as a normal session Codex No Send. Show diff (read-only). Apply in a worktree lands the changes, uncommitted, in a new worktree and opens its changes Both Open on the tool's site; Remove from Slate (it stays on the site). Neither tool offers Stop, and the doc says so Removed on the tool's site. Codex says so when asked, and the session leaves the list. The row appears within 15 seconds while the window is open, under the project holding the calling session's folder, labelled started by a scheduled task or started from another session . Codex lists only sessions Slate started. Not recorded: cloud sessions started on the web or phone, and scheduled tasks firing on their own schedule. Memory. A brought-back Claude session writes a normal transcript once you send a message. A Codex session brings back changes only; applying it notes them on the project's doc. A running cloud session has no Slate hooks and cannot reach memory, so its decisions arrive as a record (ADR 0071). On my phone # A session can continue from your phone while it runs here. Slate has no phone app: you pick it up in your tool's app. Today that is Claude Code , in the Claude app ( Code tab) or at claude.ai/code. Start on the phone : turn on On my phone in New session , above the options beside Runs on . Move a running session to the phone : On my phone at the top of its doc. Either opens a card, Ready on my phone , with three steps and the session's claude.ai link ( Copy , Open ). The same button, now blue, reopens it; Stop phone access turns it off. A phone mark shows in the list and the header counts them. Slate reads this from the transcript, so it also shows a session you put on the phone with /remote-control in your own terminal. The control is on every session, greyed out with a reason where it cannot work: Case State Claude Code running in Slate Works Claude Code in your own terminal Shown, not switched from Slate: type /remote-control there Account that cannot (API key, token, Bedrock, Vertex, or off by your organization) Greyed, with Claude's reason. Slate asks Claude ( claude doctor ) once per account Codex Not supported yet: it pairs your whole computer with the ChatGPT app, not one session Cursor, Gemini, OpenCode Cursor's phone control is in its app; Gemini and OpenCode have none It still runs here , so hooks, memory and capture work as always. While on, the conversation also goes through Anthropic (ADR 0072).

The terminal # The CLI runs on a pseudo-terminal the app owns (colours, spinners, the full TUI). Slate supplies folder, account and context and stays out of the conversation; the session is captured like any other. The CLI sees TERM_PROGRAM=Slate . Nothing is captured automatically The side panel # One panel on the right shows what the session in your active column (blue line on top) did and changed. Open by default and shared by the window; off only while that column holds no session (map, doc, plain shell). ⌥⌘B or the button at the strip's end hides it. Hidden, a button at the tab row's end brings it back, showing files waiting to commit. The choice is remembered. Drag its left edge to resize, 280 px to 640 px (never over 60% of the window); double-click for 320 px. The map icon at the end of the workspace picker's row returns to the map. Tab Shows Details (ⓘ) ⌥⌘I in a session's column, or a click on the state words in its header, opens it here Changes (⇄) Count of files waiting to commit on its icon. What the session's checkout changed ( Review the branch ); a session started in the main checkout that edits a worktree reads that worktree's changes. All files opens Projects › Code for the session's project Turns Every prompt, newest first, with when. A click scrolls the conversation to it, or finds it in terminal scrollback. A prompt that changed files shows how many; open it for the files, each opening its change. It reads the session open beside it, and runs only while this tab is picked Details # Four sections: Environment (tool, project, branch, folder, other agents there), Progress ( flow as one line such as "Check · 4 of 5", "27m in", and a bar), Context (fill; for a tool that states no window, past 200k tokens is read against a 1M window) and Links . The foot holds what the branch is for (doc, goal, documents under it), Changed , Recorded and Given . A session ends from its tab. Links is what the branch is attached to. Shut: PR #142 · #138 . Opened: a row per source mark (GitHub, Jira, Linear, Slate); click to open. The PR number comes from your remote with no sign-in. A PR's title, checks and reviews, and a GitHub issue, are read with your own gh only after you press Connect on GitHub's card; before that the card shows the number alone. The issue : a branch named for a Jira or Linear key ( SLT-138-… ) shows that item from Tasks; otherwise the GitHub issue the pull request closes, or the one whose number starts the branch name ( fix/138-… ). No commits are listed (matching by time would count a concurrent agent's work). An unjudged session stays silent. Dashed outline: not judged y

h: Agents that know about each other
x: A session you open is a tab in the same strip as your docs. Columns show several at once; a name makes one easy to find. Files, a branch's changes and previews are tabs in the same strip. Every open tab stays mounted, so switching tears no terminal down. While a session's tab shows, the rail stays on Sessions . Clicking a row opens a temporary tab (italic) that the next click replaces; a session you launch gets a kept tab. Tab gestures and keys: Tabs . Closing a session's tab ends the session, after asking. The ×, middle-click and ⌘W all ask End qa? , naming the tool still running. Choice Does End session Stops the tool, closes its terminal, removes it from the rail Close tab only Closes the tab of a hosted terminal; the session stays on the rail as "In Slate · no window" Cancel Keeps the tab Close others, Close to the right and Close all ask once, listing every session they would end. A session replaced in a temporary tab keeps running as In Slate · no window ; click its row to bring the tab back. On close the neighbouring tab takes over; with none left you land on the map. Escape, or the back arrow on a transcript, returns to the map without closing anything. Sessions in the rail returns to the session tab you were last on. ⌘-click any tab to open it in its own column: two sessions, a session and its doc, an agent beside the dev server. Sessions side by side # Open beside in a row's ⋯ , or ⌘-click on the row, shows that session in a new column right after yours. The main area holds up to 4 columns ; with four, Open beside adds a tab to the column next to yours. Each column has its own tabs. Your working column has a blue line on top; click another to work there. The list marks each session on screen with its column: left / right , middle with three, column 1 to column 4 with four. Drag the line between columns to widen one; double-click a line to equalise all. Widths are saved per workspace and survive relaunch. Back to one view: Unsplit at the top of the last column, or ⇧⌘\\. All tabs are kept. Closing a column's last tab closes the column. Naming a session # A session has one name , shown on its tab, list row and memory doc. Right-click the tab, Rename… ; Enter or clicking away keeps it, Escape keeps the old one. One line, up to 80 characters. A session with no name, or one that reads as none (blank, "session", "untitled", a raw id), shows "\‹Tool› session in \‹project›" in list, tabs, map, ⌘K and the notification. A name taken from the opening prompt leaves out what the tool wrapped round it: ‹pasted_content …› around a paste, Cursor's [Image] and ‹user_query› , a Codex preamble; a tag you typed, like ‹div› , stays. An agent run's session is named for its run. Renaming the tab renames the session in its own tool, so its resume list shows the new name: Tool How Claude Code, Codex, Cursor /rename ‹name› typed into the session OpenCode Asked through its own server Gemini Keeps no names; Slate keeps it Typed only when it cannot land in your words: the last turn ended and nothing is half-typed (if you typed and cleared, Slate waits for your next Enter or Ctrl+U). Cursor does not report turn ends: a running Cursor session gets the name when next opened in Slate (tab dimmed until then). A session in your own terminal gets it when next opened in Slate. /rename typed in any of the four CLIs updates tab, row and memory doc too. Agents that know about each other # With two or more sessions in one project, Slate tells each the others exist, once, at the start of a turn, in the message carrying the branch brief. The rail says so under the group: Told about 1 other session here , or the count of the others. Each agent gets the other's own words : tool, branch, state, what it was asked and its last message, plus the doc id. The branch goal is omitted (agents on one branch share it). Slate never says a session is running , only last active six minutes ago . It asks for nothing; the agents decide. An agent can leave one note for the others or send one to a particular agent, shown once on their next turn; a reply is another note addressed back . No inbox, scheduler or queue. Notes that only narrate progress are refused. Slate assigns nothing.

A finished worktree branch is listed as waiting for review. Open it, read every changed line, comment, then merge, keep or discard. The Changes panel commits and syncs; Turns rewinds. Branches waiting for review # A worktree branch whose agent has finished, with commits main lacks, is waiting. Slate checks every project it knows. A worktree whose session has a turn open is not waiting. Its row, under the project beside the branch, carries grey tags: Review · n files › , behind n when main moved past it, and the wait time. The row shows even when nothing runs in the project; with a session on the branch, the tag sits under that session's row. In a project with several git repositories the row names the git repository first ( editor · feat-x ). When git does not answer in time for a worktree, its row keeps the counts last read; a branch never read yet waits for the next check. The changed files and the review say git did not answer, never that the branch changed nothing. A branch main moved past cannot merge until its session rebases. With nothing running in it, it folds into a closed line at the project's end, Behind main · n (named for the branch it left, such as master ), closed on each rail redraw. Branches with a session, and kept ones, stay in view. Click the tag, or Review & merge in ⋯ , to open the review ( Reviewing the whole branch ). The header counts waiting branches ( n to review ); click it for the one waiting longest. Actions above the review: Action Does Merge into main Fast-forwards main to the branch, then removes the worktree (project's On remove runs first) and the branch. Grey until the review loads. No merge commit, no checkout. With no folder holding main only the ref moves; with one, it moves too, and the merge is refused if that folder holds uncommitted changes to a file the merge changes. Also refused: uncommitted work in the worktree, an open agent turn there, new commits since the review was drawn, and git not answering while it checks how far main moved Ask to rebase Replaces Merge when main moved. Pastes Rebase this branch on main and run the tests again. at that session's prompt (no Enter), or copies it Keep Leaves the branch; its tag becomes a grey Kept , out of the count; the button reads Unkeep . Kept is stored on this computer only. New commits from an agent make it waiting again Discard Lists every commit on no other branch that will be lost, and whether uncommitted work goes too. Confirming removes worktree and branch. Uncommitted work added after the confirm opened is refused, not removed unlisted. Also refused: open agent turn, new commits since the review was drawn Measure is against origin/main and local main (commits either holds are not the branch's work), in the tag, review, Branch changes and rail counts. The tag's count omits untracked files, so the review can list more. After Merge or Discard the next waiting branch opens, oldest first. If main moved but the worktree cannot be removed (On remove failed, or it is locked), the merge counts and a notification says why. The project's main branch is never merged or discarded here. What the branch changed # Changed is one session's own work. The panel's Changes is everything the branch holds that its base lacks, whoever wrote it: the question before a merge. It counts from where the branch left its base (later base commits never count) and includes uncommitted work . Changes shows the worktree of the agent you work in: branch once on its row, then source control. With no agent selected, each worktree with a session is a one-line section (branch, lines waiting to commit); ▸ opens it. The branch name opens the whole review. A worktree's files and search are in Projects' Code. Source control # Changes works like VS Code's Source Control; Slate runs the git. Part Behaviour Count Files waiting to commit, on the ⇄ in the header, the panel tab and the Changes title. Unpushed commits are not counted (that is Sync changes ) Fetch Automatic on opening Changes when the last fetch is over five minutes old. No fetch button Message box One line, grows as you type; rows are 24 px Main button Files to commit: full-width Commit N files , Commit & Push in its ▾ (the only two ways to commit). All committed: Sync changes , with ↑ push and ↓ pull counts; pulls, then pushes. Never pushed: Publish branch . Nothing to do: no button, Nothing to commit, and up to date. Commit Message plus every file in Changes except unticked ones and the agents' MCP, hook and settings files ( .mcp.json , .claude/settings.json …), which can hold secrets and start unticked. Nothing is staged: a file you staged stays staged and is not committed unless ticked. ⌘↵ in the message commits File row Icon, name, folder dimmed, git letter in colour (M, A, D, R); removed files struck through. Click opens the change. On hover: Open file , and ↺ restores the last commit's version (checkpoint taken first; no button undoes a discard) Folded below Outgoing · N commits , Incoming · N commits , and on a feature branch This branch vs main · N files . Never pushed: no upstream, so commits show as Not yet published · N commits against the base Every write waits for the agent. While a session works in the worktree, Commit, Sync, Publish and ↺ are off ( Claude Code is working here — waits for its turn to end ). Fetch moves no file, so never waits. Pull is a fast-forward or nothing; push never forces. If branch and upstream both moved, Sync reports git's message and leaves the branch alone. Merge or rebase in the terminal. The tree has no rename, new file, removal or drag. Reviewing the whole branch # The branch name in a worktree's section, or pointing at a rail row, opens the branch as one doc: every changed file's lines in turn, measured from the same point. The header counts files and lines added and removed. File tree (left): every changed file in its folders. A click scrolls to it and unfolds it. Viewed files are drawn quieter. Fold a file by its arrow; Fold

A session's flow says where it stands in its work. Slate works it out from the transcript and git each time the tab reads it; the agent reports nothing and nothing is stored. A build skill has five steps: Overview, Plan, Build, Check, Land . Research has three: Asked, Published, Decided . The flow shows in three places, never twice in view: on the row (a bar and the step's word, ▬▬▬▬▭ Check ), in the header ("● Working · Check"), and in Details under Progress (the goal, the bar, each step with what lit it). Reading it # The word is the step the session is in now. The bar is how far it has got. A session that ran its tests and went back to editing reads Build again, while its bar stays solid through Check. Waiting. When the latest step only waits, the word is Waiting : a sleep still running, a shell loop that sleeps until something is ready, or a scheduled wakeup. An idle session mid-step reads Waiting too. Its status is Idle and nothing pulses. Details says what it waits on, such as "sleeping". Waiting on you is the amber status, and its step keeps its own word. The bar has one colour , the accent: done steps are solid, the current step is lighter and breathes while it works, steps ahead are the grey track. Only these change a segment: Red on Check when the session stopped on a failed check. Build is current again, with "retry 1", and the words read "Check failed" (row) or "check failed" (header). While it still works, a failed check is not red: it is back at Build, fixing it. Amber on the current step while the session waits on you. Green on every segment once the work is on the default branch. There is no percent and no time left, because steps take very different times. What lights each step # Overview : the session started and is reading; it counts what it read and searched before it planned or edited. A session opened by an approved brief says "read the brief". Plan : plan mode approved in Claude Code, a todo list written (Claude Code's, Codex's update_plan ), or an approved brief opened the session. Otherwise Plan is hollow: "no plan recorded". A session that hands work out (a message to another session, a scheduled run) is at Plan and counts its "hand-offs". Build : an edit to a file in the session's own checkout. A brief in the git folder, or a file outside the checkout, is not Build, so a session that only coordinates never reads Build. After a commit it says "committed". An edit after a check or a landing moves it back to Build. Check : a test or gate run: the project's own checks (scripts, pre-push hook) or a known test runner. Land : the work is on the default branch, origin's or the local one: its last commit, or the commit its git push moved it to. It is read from git even after the worktree was removed. Its last evidence is the closing card the session sends, "card sent". Asked : research was asked. Published : it published a doc (an artifact, a Slate doc or app). Decided : your reply after it published. Where the steps come from # Each skill lists its steps in its SKILL.md frontmatter, for example flow: overview plan edit check land ( edit shows as Build). A helper skill for one part of another's work says flow: step . If the checkout is older than the skill's flow: line, the line in the git repository's main checkout is used. The skill is detected (within the first five tools) from a slash command you typed, a prompt opening with a skill's run phrase, a Skill call, or the agent reading its SKILL.md (read tool, or cat , sed , head , tail in a skills/ folder); grep / ls naming the file and tool-added skill lists do not count. A new skill's steps replace the old. With no skill, only steps that happened show, and no bar until there is more than the overview. Where the goal comes from # Slate takes the first it finds: The brief whose path the first prompt names: its title is the goal, its checklist Done when . A Markdown file of at most 64 KB inside the session's checkout or git folder. The issue : the branch is fix/‹n›-… , or the prompt says #‹n› . The branch's Plan doc in Slate: its goal. The first prompt , marked "as asked". After a slash command such as /research why… , the goal is what follows it. The notice Claude Code writes when you stop a turn is never the goal.

Slate reads a session's state from its transcript, who spoke last, and whether a running CLI process vouches for it. This guide gives the signals, the blind spots and how the list stays current. How a state is decided # A quiet transcript with no live process is a closed conversation. It leaves the tab and is never shown as Needs you . A process vouches for a session of its tool in the folder it works in (for codex --cd ‹folder› or cursor-agent --workspace ‹folder› , that folder). A session that moved on is still found by the folder it began in. Two spellings of one folder ( /tmp , /private/tmp ) count as one. A tool that lists its own sessions decides: an unlisted session is gone, but a listing alone does not prove one alive. A job the tool reports as done , stopped or failed is finished. The one exception is a widget's chat: Claude Code reports its session done after each turn while the session waits for the next message, so there done ends it only once its process is gone. A turn's last write is what touches the transcript, so a session that just asked you something reads as Working for a 45-second window. For Claude Code the window and the row's time come from the last turn, not the file: Claude Code keeps adding bookkeeping lines (cost, artifact monitors, queued messages) to a transcript long after a turn, and those do not count. A session that ended is still dated by its last write. Three signals shorten the window: The window title of a session Slate hosts. If it stops moving, the session becomes Needs you in about ten seconds. Only a title seen to move counts; of the first five CLIs only Codex animates its title. The tool's own listing , when it reports the session busy. A sub-agent still writing. This reaches a session in somebody else's terminal. For Claude Code the transcript settles it: a record with a tool call is mid-turn, one with only text is finished. A call with no result is Working , with three exceptions that read Needs you : a question to you ( AskUserQuestion ) once the 45-second window has passed; any call quiet for more than 30 minutes, which is a prompt nobody answered (a foreground command ends at its 10-minute timeout and writes a result); and, in a session Slate hosts, a quiet call whose terminal has drawn nothing (asking you to allow it). A moving title, the tool reporting busy, or a sub-agent still writing keeps it Working . Blind spots # A permission prompt in a session Slate neither hosts nor can ask reads as Working for Claude Code, for up to 30 minutes, and as idle for other tools. The exception is a Claude Code session that claude agents --json reports as waiting : it reads as Needs you , however fresh its transcript. "Waiting for permission" and "answered, waiting for your next prompt" both show as Needs you . A tool whose title does not move and whose transcript Slate cannot read this way is judged on timing alone, so a turn's end can take up to the window plus a tick to show. How it stays current # The server pushes changes ( GET /sessions/live/stream ; GET /sessions/live is the one-shot); an idle machine sends nothing. A watch re-reads only the changed transcript (150 ms coalescing), plus HEAD of each live checkout and OpenCode's database. Timers run only while needed: 5 s time passing (flips a session to Needs you ), 60 s full re-walk, 15 s process list. Your own acts (stop, closed terminal, hand-back) refresh at once ( POST /sessions/live/refresh ). Branch counts refresh at most every 30 s while sessions report, and on window focus (how an outside commit shows up).

Every agent you use shares Slate's memory. It is stored as docs you can read. Slate is an MCP server. A tool that speaks MCP (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Antigravity, OpenCode, Gemini, Cline, Grok Build, Kiro, Qwen Code, Droid, Hermes Agent, Goose, Kilo Code, Auggie) starts a session with the project's memory index, searches with recall and saves with remember . One workspace, many tools. A watcher fills it in. It reads the conversation files your agents already write and stores each session as a doc. It also reads the memory folders Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Codex keep for themselves, for the folders you added as projects. Memory is your docs. Sessions, decisions and other memories live in the same local SQLite workspace as everything else. Fix a wrong doc and the next recall reads the correction. In this section # Doc What it covers Session Capture The watcher that captures AI sessions as docs. Recall & Remember Search and citing, with links to the session brief, lessons, saving and tidying. Decisions & Memories Logged choices with rationale, and durable knowledge ranked for recall. Memory Graph Memories on the files they cite, coloured by use. The tools every AI client calls are in Slate as an MCP Server . recall reads the workspace on this machine that owns the working folder, and never leaves the machine. What you put in a shared workspace is readable by colleagues and their AI through a scope of its own, recall with scope: "workspaces" , which asks the cloud.

x: A session gets memory three ways: an index at the start, a search it runs, and a lesson on the tool call it is about. At the end it calls remember . This guide covers search and citing. Guide Covers What a session is given at the start Brief, index, other places it is given out, filter rules. Lessons Memory that arrives on the tool call it is about. remember Saving, correcting, what is refused. Tidying and measuring memory Tidy proposals, declines, lessons to skills, progress logging, measuring. recall and get_memory : search in two steps # Copy recall( query, also, cwd ) recall( query, cwd, as_of: "2026-08-01" ) get_memory( refs ) recall searches the project's memories, its docs in Slate, and the project's own files, and returns one line per memory with ref and citation. The project's own files are the ones at the root of the project folder the cwd is in (the nearest folder holding .git : AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md , README.md , CONTRIBUTING.md ) and every .md file under docs/ , doc/ , adr/ and decisions/ , read from disk on each call, for any project, not only Slate. A file hit carries its path in the project folder; read the file for the whole text. It comes after the memories unless it matches the question at least twice as well as the best memory does. A tool asks with the person's question in query , as asked, and 3–6 keywords of its own as the first entry of also ; the question is never replaced by the keywords. It gets a shortlist: 15 candidates by default, 25 at most, memories and files together, best first, each one line with its id or path and kind. After the list comes one line asking it to pick the ones that answer its task, or say none fits, and to pass the refs it relied on in used on its next recall , remember or log_mission_progress , never in its reply. The choosing is the AI's. Measured on real sessions ( yarn memory:gate , ADR 0130), the session's AI picked a right item as often from this list as from the old 8, and handled more questions nothing answers when the list kept the cut below. The app's own calls (the in-app agent, a task's memory) get 8 results, memories at most half, docs the rest. When the query is about the branch (it names the branch, or asks what is open or in progress) the first result is the branch brief: goal, open items, recent sessions and commits, from records labelled with the branch and from git. A memory scoring under 0.7 of the best memory's score is left out, on a tool's shortlist too; the best one always stays. A doc matches by one section: the doc is cut at its headings, and a section counts when it, with the doc's title and its own heading, covers the query's rarest words (a title or heading word counts more than a body word). Words scattered over a long doc do not make it a match. A doc found by its title alone is not returned, and neither is a log: a captured session, or a doc an older Slate wrote as a running session log or a pile of old notes ("Session log — …", "Earlier notes on main, …"). Those stay in the app and its search. kind: "docs" searches doc text only, up to 20 results, logs left out. When nothing matches well enough, recall says so in one line and names up to three docs whose titles match, as places to read, never as answers. Every recall is logged with how many memories and docs it returned, the empty ones too, so Slate can count the sessions that looked something up and found nothing. When the session ends, its transcript ties each of its lookups to it, and a memory it names afterwards counts as that lookup's use. How results are ranked # Memories are ranked lexically and locally with BM25. No model is called and nothing is downloaded. Each query word counts by its rarity among your memories. Sentence and keywords (count most), reason, tags and citation are read, in that order of weight; words match by stem ("refused" finds "refusal"), and case, accents and punctuation do not matter ("preproduction" finds "préproduction"). remember takes keywords : 5 to 10 words or short phrases a later question would use that the sentence does not (synonyms, other names, an acronym and its spelling out). They count like the sentence, and only for the memory they are written on: a query is never widened with another memory's keywords. Recent memories are lifted slightly; a newer near-tie on the same subject comes first. From 200 memories in a workspace, a match is lifted (at most doubled) by how close its words sit to the query's in your store (latent semantic analysis, fitted in memory). It only re-orders keyword matches; a memory sharing no word is never added. Your acts on the code move a match, at most doubled or halved: merges and Confirms lift, reverts and discards of the code its sessions wrote lower (see Citing ). Nothing found is an answer. From 50 memories in a project, a memory covering too little of the query is not returned, so an unanswerable question gets none. A barely passing memory is marked weak . citation: changed or citation: gone (file missing) means read the code before relying on it. The cited file is read in the session's checkout first, then the project's folder, so a worktree session checks against its branch. Second search. also takes up to three other phrasings; each is searched alone and results merged. Use after a thin first search. The past. as_of answers from what memory believed at the end of that day (UTC; no zone means UTC), including claims replaced since; each carries until . Memories only (a doc keeps just its current text). Use it for "what did we decide back then", not for work you are about to do. It does not count as memory offered to a session. get_memory # Field Meaning reason Why it was written. source_ref The file or commit it is about. citation same : cited code unchanged (for a line range or symbol, those lines, found again after edits above; for a bare file, the whole file). changed : check the code first. gone : file missing. unchecked : nothing to compare. status , pinned , written , cited

A terminal session is matched by working directory. A broken Slate. Enforcement fails open: an unreadable setting or a crashed hook lets the prompt through. When some did not: "1 of 3 captured sessions ran under an account this project does not assign." Review lists up to five, each with the account it ran under and the one expected. Contents # The approval card Autonomy A plan or a question Stop What Home shows about the agent What differs by agent The approval card # The agent can read files, edit files and run shell commands in the project you scoped the turn to. It asks first , in the amber card used for workspace writes. The card shows the tool's call and the full argument (the whole shell command), with three answers: Answer Effect Approve Runs this one call; nothing is remembered Always allow Runs it and keeps a rule so the next identical call is not asked. Claude Code: saved to the project's .claude/settings.local.json (the card prints the exact rule first). Codex: remembered for the session. Cursor, OpenCode: kept in their own allowlist Skip Refuses and tells the agent why, so the reply says the call was declined A box beside Skip takes an optional reason, which can become a memory proposal. Always allow appears only when the CLI offered a rule. A question card has no Approve : each answer is a button. Several calls at once queue and show one at a time. An answer belongs to its own card, so a double click cannot approve the next one unseen. Slate's own tools (reading docs, writing memory) skip the card. Everything else asks, including MCP servers you connected. Background work (an automation's run) shows no card while running. Its rules decide, and a call that changes something is held and appears on Home as an Automation asks card after the run ( Automations ). Autonomy # The autonomy pill sets how much skips the card. The ⌘J panel and Home's composer share it. Setting Effect Ask first Asks before every file edit and command Auto-edit Applies file edits; asks before a shell command Full auto Asks about nothing A click moves one step; entering Full auto needs a second click. New chat resets to Ask first. A change applies to the current conversation with no restart, so no tool signs in again. Create an automation and Run an automation ignore the pill and always ask, because they spend money. Other Slate writes (a new doc) run without asking under Auto-edit and Full auto. A plan or a question # Plan. The tool writes the whole plan and shows it before touching anything. Approve starts it; Skip keeps planning. Question. When the tool needs a decision, each offered answer is a button; picking one answers. The CLI hides its plan and question tools from hosts that cannot answer them; Slate can. Stop # Stop ends the turn and keeps the agent running with its connections, so your next message needs no new sign-ins. A message sent right after waits up to 10 seconds for the stopped turn to let go, then starts a fresh one. A tool that runs one process per message has it ended ( fallback ). Stop also declines every waiting card; an interrupted step reads Stopped. Home has one warm agent. A chat started with Chat in Sessions has its own, in its own folder; Stop, mode and model there reach only that tool, and closing its tab ends it ( A chat instead of a terminal ). What Home shows about the agent # The reply streams as written. A context meter by the token count shows how full the tool's window is (share and bar), using the CLI's numbers (matches /context ). It refreshes each turn, darkens from 75%, and shows tokens only if the size is unknown. The top bar's tools chip shows connecting agents… with a spinner during the first turn, then how many MCP servers the tool reported (names on hover, · 1 failed in amber for any that did not connect). A hook that blocks a turn is reported in the chat with its name and reason. Only failing hooks are reported. / lists skills and commands ( Skills and mentions ). Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini, GitHub Copilot and the ten newest (Antigravity, Cline, Grok Build, Kiro, Qwen Code, Droid, Hermes Agent, Goose, Kilo Code, Auggie) speak the Agent Client Protocol. Approval cards work on Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode. For the ten newest, Home, Stop, the model picker and the approval card are unverified : only their ACP handshake was checked. Full table: Features by Agent . Claude Code Codex Asks before a command, file change or tool yes yes Question with options as buttons yes yes Plan to approve yes — Always allow saves a project rule remembers for the session Stop ends the turn, not the tool yes yes Context meter, model picker, streaming yes yes Own slash commands in / after the first reply yes — (in its terminal UI, not the protocol) Codex also asks before escalating out of its sandbox and passes on questions from its own connected MCP servers . GitHub # Read through the GitHub CLI ( gh ) once you press Connect on its card in Connect → Integrations or setup. A signed-in gh alone reads nothing. Several gh accounts: Slate asks gh who is signed in, in every gh config folder, including several logins in one folder ( gh auth login twice, gh auth switch ). Each workspace reads as the account owning its git repositories (for an organisation's, the one that can see them). A workspace no account reaches shows no GitHub; switching accounts drops the old one's tasks. A remote cloned through an SSH host alias ( git@github.com-work:acme/app ) counts as GitHub: the alias is resolved with ssh -G .
