Accounts and models are set in Connect → Agents. A group's or project's tools override the workspace's; a new project asks for none. A refused action # A failed move, rename, duplicate, Move to Trash or restore (doc gone, workspace read-only, someone else's doc) shows a bottom message naming the doc and reason; the tree stays as it was. It closes after 8 seconds (waits while pointed at) or with ✕. The same message reports what you did elsewhere, with Undo when possible.

Code lists every project with a git folder on this computer (the picked one, or all) with two views on its left edge: Files and Changes . A project with no folder here says so. Open it with Code on a project's doc ( The doc tree ). Files # A tree like an editor's explorer. One-folder project: one row (name and branch) with files under it. With one project picked the row goes: files start at the top under a bar with the branch and the row's buttons. Two or more git worktrees: a group headed like slate · 2 worktrees , a row per worktree named by branch (hover for folder). Group starts open, worktrees shut; all stays as left. Files changed since the last commit show M , A or D , with a dot on their folders. Find a file by name with ⌘K. Hover a checkout's row: New file , New folder , Refresh , Collapse all . Right-click a file, folder or the space below: New file , New folder , Open terminal here , Start session here , Copy path , Reveal in Finder , Rename , Move to Trash . Names are typed in place. These wait while an agent works in that project. Rename or trash can be undone from its message or from Turns; a trashed file is also in the system Trash (the Recycle Bin on Windows). A file on another disk than the Trash, or on a Windows network share or removable drive, is refused and stays where it was. Changes # One section per checkout with files waiting to be committed, named by project and branch (branch named once). Source control as VS Code lays it out: one-line message, full-width Commit with Commit & Push in its ▾, files waiting (each committed unless unticked), same as a session's Changes ( Sessions ). The icon counts all waiting files. A worktree removed in a terminal leaves the list within about half a minute, or at once on returning to the window. A file in a tab # A file opens in a tab; the rail stays on Projects. A file picked in ⌘K comes here with its tree unfolded. The line under the cursor shows, after its end, when it last changed and in which commit. Blame shows it for every line. Show changes appears when the file differs from where its branch began; Back to the file or Esc leaves. Bottom bar: branch, worktree when relevant, path from the project folder.

doc_type says what kind a doc is; status says where it stands. Together they give memory tools a structure to navigate. Doc types # A new doc is a plain Doc . The chip under the title ( Doc ▾ ) changes its type any time, listing the seven types a person writes: Doc, Plan, Design, Review, Meeting, Test Plan, Bug Report. A change appends the new type's template headings after the existing text, once. Group, project and branch are made by Slate from folders and sessions, so they are not in the menu. The DocType enum is in @slate/schema ( doc-type/types.ts ): DocType Purpose general Plain knowledge doc design Design doc plan Implementation or work plan review Review write-up meeting Meeting notes test-plan Test plan bug-report Bug report group Set of projects you made and named; no folder of its own project One folder, usually a git repository, in a group or alone mission Legacy; work now files under its project ( mission docs ) Status # From DOC_STATUSES : draft (started, not active), active (in progress), done , canceled (abandoned). The hierarchy # Structural types nest as memory expects ( @slate/schema , doc-type/rules.ts ): Copy group └── project └── branch └── knowledge docs (plan | design | test-plan | bug-report | review | meeting | general) A project may stand at top level with no group. Knowledge docs may sit directly under a group or project . ALLOWED_DOC_CHILDREN says what nests under what; for groups, projects and branches it is enforced on move (a project dropped in a branch is refused). A knowledge doc in an unusual place shows a tree warning. Memory tools work without a doc id: on recall or remember Slate resolves a target by walking from the current project and group. A memory belongs to the project it concerns and says which git branch it was learned on (a label, never a doc). A decision's full reasoning is a decision doc under the project, labelled with its branch; the tree counts them in a Decisions row. Filling one in # Slate never creates a knowledge doc without asking: at a milestone your agent asks whether to save it ( mission docs ). To have an agent write into a doc, use Start session on the doc's header or its Sessions tab. The launcher hands the CLI the doc, its lineage (group → project → branch), the branch's goal and next open item, and the project's recorded decisions ( Sessions → Starting a session from a doc ). See also: Docs & the Block Editor , Recall & Remember .

h: Slate offers the doc at each milestone
x: A mission doc was Slate's first container for a piece of work. No new ones are made; old ones still open. Work now files under its project : a session, plan or decision made on a git branch carries the branch as a label, and no doc stands for the branch. An old mission doc ( doc_type = mission ) keeps nesting, breadcrumbs and the editor, and: the type chip shows its status : draft , active , done , canceled ; a new empty one starts from the old outline: Goal, Checklist, Session log, Decisions, Notes; a list above the text shows docs filed under it; a project may hold one without a tree warning. The Doc ▾ menu does not offer mission ( Typed Docs ). Progress on a branch # The next session on a branch, yours or an agent's, starts with what the branch is for, derived from the project's records labelled with the branch and from git. No doc holds it. The MCP tool log_mission_progress takes cwd (and branch when the work was on a branch other than the checked-out one, which git must know): Copy recall → work the task → log_mission_progress(summary, goal, open_items, decisions) Goal and open items become the branch's goal and open items, shown in the next session's brief. A newer report replaces the older; they fade after a state memory's shelf life, and are retired when the branch lands or is removed. Each decision is saved as a decision memory labelled with the branch. The summary is a session entry of the project, labelled with the branch, in its Sessions tab. No doc is made. On a trunk branch ( main , master , develop ) the goal is not changed. log_mission_progress is a memory tool exposed to every connected agent ( Recall & Remember ). Slate offers the doc at each milestone # At a milestone (plan, review, test plan, bug report, design) Slate has your agent ask in chat whether to keep it as a doc. It tells the tool to use its own click-to-answer question tool, so where that tool shows choices you click one; the wording is the tool's. Tool Asks with Reminded when you ask for a milestone Sent back to ask if a plan was never offered Claude Code AskUserQuestion yes yes Gemini CLI ask_user yes yes Codex request_user_input yes yes OpenCode question yes yes; its end-of-turn event cannot reply, so Slate's plugin sends the ask as a new prompt when the turn goes idle Cursor AskQuestion sent from Cursor's prompt event, which does not run in print mode ( cursor-agent -p ) yes in the interactive app; its stop event does not run in print mode Choose save and the tool saves the doc in the project, labelled with the branch; choose not and nothing is saved. If the branch already has that doc, the choice is to add to it, keeping what is there. Every tool also carries a standing instruction to ask before saving a plan, review, test plan, bug report or design. A plan from plan mode is kept as the branch's Plan doc, in the project, labelled with the branch. A later plan on the same branch replaces the one Slate made. A Plan doc you wrote is never changed. See also: Typed Docs & Hierarchy , Recall & Remember , Docs & the Block Editor .

An automation works without being driven: a standup at 7:00, a debrief when a coding session ends, a plan per assigned ticket. Automations holds yours and everything they write, plus what Slate runs itself ( Built-in ). Make an automation # An automation is a job, a trigger and steps , held to rules . Click + in the side panel's title row. Pick From a template , Set it up yourself (empty editor) or Describe it to AI… (an agent writes it). Write the Job in your words ("Every weekday morning, tell me where each project stands and what to focus on"). Every step reads it first; with none, steps run as written. Pick what starts it, and a project. What starts it # Starts When By hand Run now . You can type a starting text. On a schedule How often : every day , every weekday , every week or every month , at an hour and minute :00, :15, :30 or :45. Weekday = Monday to Friday (a weekend run moves to Monday, same time). Monthly takes day 1 to 28. Listed as "Weekdays · 7:30 AM". When a session ends After an AI coding session is captured. With Scheduled automations off in Automations › Built-in these do not start, nor later for sessions that ended meanwhile. When a task arrives When Tasks pulls in a new integration item, such as an assigned ticket. One read hands the run up to 5 new items. If already running, new items wait and start one run together afterwards. A just-connected tracker starts nothing (its first read brings everything). Your own to-dos never start one. Tasks reads integrations on opening and on returning to the window after over a minute. Starts on its own only while Runs on its own (under Starts ) is on. A line under the schedule says "Next: Mon 7:30 AM" or "Off, so it will not run on its own." Any automation can be run by hand. Your agent can run one too, from whichever tool you are in ("run my morning report"): its run_automation tool lists your automations and starts one, as Run now does, while Slate is open. That run asks before it changes anything, like any other. Making or changing an automation stays here ( Tool Reference ). Asleep at due time : runs once on wake. For time-bound reports switch on Skip a run that is more than two hours late ("· skips late runs"). One at a time ; never started twice. Slate stops mid-run : marked failed; a scheduled one reruns minutes after return. An automation belongs to the workspace it was made in and runs on this computer while Slate runs, in every workspace, with or without a window. An automation in a shared workspace runs only on the computer of the person who made it: automations do not sync, so teammates never have a copy to run. One that runs when a session ends starts for a session in its workspace's folders. It needs a project: New ones open in the project Automations is narrowed to and cannot be saved without one. With none picked, Runs in says Pick a project , listing only groups and projects. The six seeded ones have no project: Run now and Turn on ask, save, then go on. Turn off never asks. No scheduled run without a project. If the project was removed: editable and can be switched off, not on, until you pick one. Moving a group or project to another workspace takes its automations along. Its steps # Run in order; each reads what came before: @context : what the run started with: text typed at Run now, "A coding session just ended.", or today's date for a scheduled run. After Recent tasks, that step's report. @prev : previous step's answer. A step can name its own agent (one on Claude, next on Gemini); none named uses the automation's tool, with the account from the group or project. Each run writes one report : last step's answer first, earlier steps after under their labels. The first step can be Recent tasks : Recent tasks . What it follows # Follows , in the editor under Runs in : Slate's own steps : as written (default). A skill of its project ( Skills in project ): the skills Toolkit shows. A subagent of its project ( Subagents ). + New skill in Toolkit… : opens Toolkit's New skill form on the project with name and purpose filled. Create writes it, sets the automation to follow it, returns you. Only for a saved automation with no unsaved changes. Every step opens the skill's or subagent's file first and follows it, so runs count as that skill's use. The file is found in the project's folder at run start. If the skill left the project, the editor says so and runs follow Slate's own steps until you pick another. Moving the automation to another project clears the choice. The thread # Opens on its Thread : every run, oldest first; typed words above the answer they started; under each run a line of what it used ("Used jira ×2, github · 1 call waiting for you"). A report over 1,600 characters shows its opening; Read the whole report opens it. To answer the last run, type in the box under the thread and press Send : one more short run (not the steps) on the same agent and folder, reading the last four turns and your words, each earlier report cut to its first 3,000 characters. The box is off while the automation runs or cannot run (for example, no project). Before the first run it is the run's starting text and the button says Start ; Run now runs with nothing typed. What it may do # An automation uses the tools its agent reaches: your MCP servers (Jira, GitHub, Slack…). Setup → May do : Reading goes on without asking : searching, listing, opening a ticket or pull request. A call that changes something asks first : posting, commenting, creating an issue. Merging, removing and writing files are refused. It also reads apps connected in Connect → Integrations with no MCP server needed ( connected_tools , read_connected , using Slate's sign-in). Setup shows each at the head of the Allowed row with its logo; click opens Connect. Excluded: token-connected apps, and an app the automation's Deny covers whole ( mcp__linear__* ). The report names the app ( linear · list_issues ) and the lists below treat that read as a call to it. Three

Recent tasks is a first step for an automation . Before writing it gathers what happened and checks it against your live tools. Only the first step can be one, since later steps read its report. Context it sees # Source Brings in Sessions Up to 80 newest captured AI sessions in the look-back window, tagged with group or project; one-line summary cut at 280 characters Memories Up to 30 memories picked by pin, recent use and kind (not date), each with kind ( decision / preference / state / fact / lesson ), ref and reasoning; list stops at about 5,600 characters; memories whose cited code changed are left out. Scoped to a group or project: that doc's own memory (a group's includes its projects'), plus global Docs Titles of up to 100 docs, newest change first, in the automation's group or project Prior runs Its own three latest reports, each's opening 600 characters Look back : days of sessions read, 1 to 365, starting at 7. Write decisions back to memory : the report may end with a memories block, saved as memory (at most five per run) and removed from the report you read. The same switch lets a memory-proposals block propose merges and retirements of the memories shown, by ref; each waits in Memory under Needs review until accepted. Only an automation scoped to a group or project can file one. It can also search the workspace and your connected tools; what it may change follows the automation's rules ( What it may do ). Grounding on live tools # Stored records show what was true when written, so Recent tasks checks live tools first. It takes the distinct working contexts (directory and CLI config) of the period's sessions, drops folders under /tmp and similar, ranks the rest (git checkouts first, then work done), keeps the top three, and names the others as skipped. For each, one short pass runs the agent in that directory under that config (so project-scoped MCP servers load), checking: Jira or Linear: your issues, not Done (defines your work). GitHub: your pull requests for those tickets: state, CI, who the review waits on. Calendar: today's meetings (skipped if the calendar was already read). Slack: who waits on what for those tickets and pull requests, last three days. Passes ask only for identifiers, states, names and times. Ticket bodies, comments and message text are never requested or stored. The report # Opens with three columns: Assigned to me , Pull requests , Today's meetings . A pull request shows its full GitHub name ( acme/api#12 ), so two projects' #12 are two rows. A source needing sign-in shows a sign-in button (same account and directory as the pass), then reruns the automation. An unreachable source says so, never "Nothing assigned". The text then lists what was verified this run and which sources could not be reached (the agent said so, or its CLI reported the server failed, pending, unknown or needing sign-in). If no project had sessions in the window nothing is checked, and the report says so. A ticket or PR status may be stated as current only if a tool returned it this run. Seeded Standup and Shutdown end with Not verified ; a gallery template adds none unless its prompt does. Prompt variables # Filled just before it runs; only Recent tasks reads them (the editor warns if a later step uses one and points to @context ): Variable Expands to @sessions Recent captured sessions @memory Memories the run is given: up to 30, each with kind, ref and reason. Never a hidden memory or a stale state . If Slate's server is not running, the line says no memory @docs The doc titles above @date Today's date @prior_outputs Recent reports of this automation

Slate runs thirteen things on its own; Automations › Built-in (the row under Overview in Automations ) says what each does and what turning it off costs. Eleven have a switch. Two always run: clearing the queue a finished session leaves, and the startup repairs . Switch scope # Ten switches are app-wide: off stops it in every workspace. They pause things you already choose one by one (each automation's switch, each reminder, each workspace's sharing) all at once. AI memory care is per workspace: it spends your agent's tokens on that workspace's account. Its card is last in Built-in and says it holds for this workspace only. Auto-capture appears twice (top card and a list row): one switch. What runs # Automation Does Off means Scheduled automations Starts your automations at their times and those that run when a session ends; files each report under its group or project. Every workspace on this computer, while Slate runs (window open or not) and the computer is awake Nothing runs on a schedule; automations stay listed and run by hand Shared workspace sync At startup, then every two minutes: pushes your docs in a shared workspace, pulls others'. Needs sign-in. After repeated failures waits longer, up to an hour Shared workspaces stop updating both ways; Sync now still works agent runs Adds Run with AI… to a task (branch, folder, guided run). Every two minutes checks if a shipped run's pull request merged; for 30 days after shipping, hourly checks for a revert Task card offers only Just open a session ; started runs keep their rules; no merge or revert checks Reminders Rings when a task with a time comes due, in every workspace on this computer Nothing rings; times stay AI memory care (per workspace) Below Free rules only: memories whose code is gone or whose state expired are hidden, badly shaped new ones refused; nothing spent Automatic updates Checks for a version, downloads in background, installs on next quit Keep your version until you check in Settings → About Tell me when a session needs me One notification when a session waits on a permission or question and Slate is not in front; none for a finished turn Sessions carry on; the amber dot and ⌘⇧J show the waiting one Show Slate in the menu bar Menu bar icon opens a panel of working or waiting sessions, with a count while one needs you Icon leaves; Sessions and ⌘⇧J still show all Start Slate at login Off until you choose. Setup offers it ticked; an older install asks once. Starts Slate in the menu bar at login, with no window , so every agent can reach it Starts only when you open it; until then agents cannot reach Slate Auto-capture Watches agents' transcripts and your projects, files what happens into the workspace owning the folder. While Slate is open; sessions run after quitting are caught at next launch Nothing captured on its own, at once; agents can still write through Slate's MCP server Keep the computer awake Off until turned on. While a session or automation works, stops the computer sleeping Computer sleeps on schedule; running work pauses until wake Per-agent capture. Auto-capture is the master switch. Each agent whose transcripts Slate reads has a Capture switch on its row in Connect → Agents : off, its sessions are not recorded; it stays connected; other tools unaffected. Cursor has none: its capture is the hook on that row. A switch applies on the next tick, not next launch: within a minute for the automation tick, two for sync and the merge check. Auto-capture applies at once. AI memory care # Off until turned on. Each night at 03:00, with the computer awake and Slate open, it reads up to 50 memories the free rules cannot judge. Each is read twice, separately, against the code it cites. Skipped: pinned or protected memories, lessons with a trigger, preferences, memories with a proposal waiting, any read in the last 90 days. One group or project per night: the one with the most memories, on its own agent and account. A memory both readings call wrong is retired ( Bring back under the retired chip in Memory undoes it for 30 days). A disagreement waits in Memory → Needs review , at most 10 at once. Turning it on shows the cost and asks a monthly token cap: 1 million, 4 million or none. It stops for the month when the next night would pass it. Runs as an automation named Memory care , so Scheduled automations must be on. What reaches the network # Slate's own account ( Privacy & Security ): the update check (release manifest) and shared-workspace sync. Through your agent's CLI, under its auth : scheduled automations, session-end automations, agent runs, AI memory care. Your own gh or glab : agent run merge check and revert search (revert search is GitHub only). Everything else is local. Turning something off removes nothing: capture off keeps captured sessions; sync off does not withdraw shared docs ( leaving a workspace ). Starting at login # Your agents reach Slate's memory, skills and connections through its MCP server, and that server runs only while Slate does. So Slate can start when you log in. Only if you chose it. Setup shows Start Slate in the menu bar when you log in on the Agents step, ticked; untick it to say no. If you installed Slate before this existed, or skipped setup before that step, Slate asks once in a strip at the top of the window: Turn on or Not now . Either answer is kept, and you are not asked again. Until you answer, Slate adds no login item. macOS's own login item. Slate registers itself with macOS (SMAppService), so it shows under its own name in System Settings → General → Login Items , and you can turn it off there too. If macOS waits for you to allow it, the switch says so, with Open Login Items . No window. A login launch starts only the menu bar icon and the server; it does not even load the window. The Dock icon, the menu bar panel, opening Slate again, or a slate:// link opens the window. If you are signed out, the window opens at once, because Slate needs you to sign in. Older login

An artifact is a web page an agent made for you: an HTML page, dashboard, chart, report or Markdown note. Any connected tool publishes one with the publish_artifact MCP tool; it is stored in your workspace on this computer and listed in Artifacts in the rail. A widget is different ( get_widget , publish_widget ); given a widget, the artifact tools refuse and name those. Make or change one # You ask; you never edit by hand. Ask for one : "make me a dashboard of this data as an artifact". Every connected tool is also told to show a chart, table or report this way unprompted. Ask for a change : "make the bars blue", in Ask for a change under the title or to any tool. Open it : click the slate://artifacts link the tool gives; it names the workspace, so Slate switches first. Details: The tool sends the HTML with a title, or writes a file and sends its path. Files are read only from the working folder or a temp folder, never a file or folder whose name starts with a dot below your home or the working folder ( .env , .ssh ). A working folder that is your home folder or wider is not trusted. Ask for a change opens a session in the artifact's project, on that project's tool. It reads the HTML with get_artifact and sends only the changed parts. That adds a version ; older stay. Republishing the same HTML adds none. On an older version the box says so ("This change starts from v1, not the newest (v3)") and the tool sends the whole HTML as a new version (edits apply only to the newest). The Artifacts screen # Side panel : Overview , then every artifact in the workspace, newest first, with an HTML or Markdown icon and last-change time. Artifacts belong to the workspace, so no project picker. Filter artifacts matches title and description. Overview : a card per artifact, newest first, the same cards Widgets draws. An HTML picture is the HTML in a script-free frame in Slate's look and the current theme; script-drawn charts show only what the markup holds. Markdown uses the viewer's renderer. Drawn only while on screen, at most nine at a time. Open artifact : name, who made it and when, what it is. Preview | Code : the HTML or its read-only source (HTML laid out one block per line, indented; only spacing changes). Copy HTML copies the HTML as published. ‹ v2 of 3 › : steps versions. An older one says "You are looking at v2. The newest is v3." with Restore this version (republishes it as a new version; nothing in between is lost). Ask for a change shows only on an artifact you published under a project folder (a teammate's has one writer; a folderless one has nowhere to start a session). ⋯ : Copy HTML or Copy Markdown , Open in browser (HTML only), Rename , Delete forever (asks "Delete every version forever?"). A failed rename or removal keeps the menu open with the reason. Finding one # ⌘K : title or description, and Markdown by text, under ARTIFACTS after reports. HTML code is not searched. The doc it was made on : Artifacts made here . A branch shows its own; a project every one made inside it. recall : returns up to 2 artifacts after memories when every word of the question matches one, so a session can find last week's dashboard and change it. How HTML artifacts look # Slate's look (app font, colours, plain buttons, inputs, tables, code, headings; your theme, Mint or Forest, live) comes before the artifact's own styles, which win. In your own browser: default colours and the system light or dark. Tools are told to use var(--text) , var(--muted) , var(--surface) , var(--border) , var(--accent) , chart colours var(--c1) to var(--c5) , and classes card , badge , grid , row , stack . Live artifacts # Published with live: true , an artifact reads your workspace while shown, so a dashboard stays current without republishing. Header: Reads your workspace · no internet . Toggling live adds a version (ADR 0070). Aspect Rule Reads Docs, one doc's text, memories and AI sessions of its project (whole workspace if made under none); newest first, up to 5,000 rows each; read-only Network No fetch, WebRTC, resource hint (preconnect, prefetch), internet image or font, form, new window, frame or document.write . Scripts may load from cdnjs, jsDelivr, unpkg (chart libraries work). An attempt to leave for another address closes it Isolation No origin of its own; shares nothing with other artifacts, not even localStorage; talks to Slate only over a private channel opened at start Yours only In a shared workspace a teammate's live artifact is a plain HTML page and never reads your store; restored on another computer it is also plain Where it runs # HTML runs its own scripts, served from your workspace on a private local address apart from Slate and your data; it cannot steer the Slate window and nothing is copied to disk. It may load internet scripts and fonts. Markdown is formatted text. A teammate's artifact has no storage of its own (scripts, forms, downloads, popups kept) and cannot read the browser storage of your own artifacts, which keep theirs. In a shared workspace every member sees artifacts. One writer, the publisher: a teammate's shows "Written by" and their name, with no Rename or Delete forever. Their new versions reach you on next sync, newest only; you keep versions received; later joiners start at the newest. Moving a group or project to another workspace takes its artifacts along. Limits # One web page per artifact, up to 5,000,000 characters. HTML or Markdown only.

h: What a widget writes stays the widget's
x: A widget is a small card that Slate runs for you: tokens per project, a review queue, a form that files tasks. You describe it, your agent writes it, and it shows on a tab: today Activity , Home , or the side panel of a session open in Sessions . Change it by asking again, or by editing its files. A widget is a small folder of React files, built on @slate/sdk and @slate/ui . It is an artifact with its own Widgets item on the rail. Every version is kept. The starter Slate makes a new widget from ("Your agent is building this widget…") is not one: your agent's first build is version 1, and a new version comes only when you ask for a change. There is one kind of widget. Decisions: ADR 0077, ADR 0089 and, for GitHub, ADR 0080. Contents # Making one Showing one Using and changing one What it can read What it can ask for Reading through your MCP tools What a widget writes stays the widget's What it cannot do When Slate updates For the agent building it Limits Making one # Open Widgets . With no widget open you see the Overview : a box at the top, then your widgets as cards, two to a row. Before your first widget, "What should Slate show you?" stands above the box. Pick the tab under Show it on (it starts on the first tab with room), then describe the widget ("Describe a widget for Activity…") and press the arrow (or Enter). The box names the agent that builds it, your workspace's tool from Connect → Agents; press it to pick another. A card and a list row appear at once, marked Building : "Claude Code is writing App.tsx" while a file is written, else "Building…". When done, the card shows the widget's age, or Failed if the last build did not pass. Once its AI session starts, the widget opens, with the chat beside its preview, so you watch it being built. Each card shows a still picture of the widget, kept for the 24 widgets shown most recently. While your agent works on a widget it already built, the card keeps showing it, with the Building line over the picture. Without one for the current version, Slate runs the widget once, unseen, in the sealed Preview frame (nine cards at most at once). A pulsing doc shape shows meanwhile, then the widget's glyph after 12 seconds. The work runs in a session Slate keeps in the background, under your own agent and account. You never see its terminal: the chat shows the conversation in Slate's own words. It does not open in Sessions. Your next message goes on in the same conversation, for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI and Copilot CLI, which each continue a conversation by its id. With any other agent, a message after its session ended starts a new conversation; the widget's own folder (its WIDGET.md and code) tells it what was built. If your agent no longer has the conversation (its transcript is gone, or it cannot resume it), Slate starts a new one with the same message, once. A widget belongs to the workspace, not a project. The rail lists every widget in the workspace. Each gets a work folder on this computer ( sessions/‹workspace›/widgets/‹widget id› ), never synced; the tool writes the widget through Slate, not into it. Delete forever removes that folder. Slate marks it trusted so tools skip "trust this folder?". If your agent asks something the chat cannot turn into buttons (a sign-in, a question with no card yet), the header says Asking you and the chat shows one line: "Claude Code needs an answer Slate cannot show here." (your tool's name), with Open in Sessions . If no session shows up within 30 seconds of your message, the line says it has not started yet, with the same button. A turn that ended is Done , never Asking you . Showing one # Slate owns the card; the widget only fills it. A widget shows on its tab only at a size it was seen to fit: A few per tab. Home shows at most 3 widgets, Activity at most 2, and a session's side panel 1, as one more tab beside Details, Changes and Turns. Each widget runs in its own sealed frame, a whole web page of its own, so each one costs memory and a render. Home is for the one thing that needs you, and a wall of widgets would bury it. The tool's own uninstall removes it all. The MCP server is separate: every tool reaches it through one slate entry in its config. OpenCode and GitHub Copilot have no plugin route, so hooks go into their config. So for Claude Code, Gemini and Cursor when the plugin cannot be installed or run. Codex takes no config hooks. Without its plugin it keeps only the MCP entry. The MCP entry is a URL on the running app ( http://127.0.0.1:47366/mcp ; the port follows the Mac user, 47366 for the first account) with Slate's private key in a header (ADR 0106). No session starts its own process. Slate writes the entry itself, readable by you only. Claude Desktop and VS Code keep a stdio entry running slate-mcp . VS Code's entry goes into each of VS Code, VS Code Insiders and VSCodium that is installed, and into the own mcp.json of every VS Code profile; on Linux their folders follow XDG_CONFIG_HOME . A profile made after you connect gets the entry when VS Code is next turned on in Connect. With Slate closed the tool lists the server as failed and the session-start hook says why: open Slate, start a new session. Tool Turning it on Claude Code installs the plugin Codex installs the plugin Gemini installs the plugin, as a Gemini extension Cursor installs the plugin, as a link in Cursor's local plugins folder OpenCode writes one plugin module and names it in OpenCode's config (OpenCode loads a module, not a directory) GitHub Copilot writes the slate entry into ~/.copilot/mcp-config.json and hooks into ~/.copilot/hooks/slate.json , a file of its own The ten newest tools write the slate entry into the tool's own MCP config (the file is in the tool's record in agentsAndHosts.json ). Grok Build, Droid, Hermes Agent and Auggie also get hooks; Antigravity, Kiro, Cline and Goose get none yet Node 24 or newer is needed for the plugin. Without it, tools with a config route use that. If Node disappears, Slate removes the plugin rather than leave a server that cannot start. Slate asks your shell once per launch where node is (an app opened from Finder has no shell PATH), which finds fnm, nvm, volta and asdf. Only from where Slate lives. Opened straight from the disk image, or from the temporary copy macOS runs a downloaded app from, Slate installs no plugin: that path is gone once the app moves, and the tool would keep a dead link. The config route carries capture until Slate runs from Applications (or any folder or drive it was copied to); a registration left from such a copy is recognised as Slate's and replaced then. Exactly one way. Each launch checks every tool and profile: with the plugin installed, old hooks are removed; a connected tool with neither gets back what it can have (else everything runs twice). Slate decides from its record of what it installed per profile: a matching profile gets no writes, an unrecorded one is left alone unless you connected it, and a connected profile that lost Slate is connected again. Only turning it off in Connect keeps it off. If Slate's record, or its list of connected or turned-off profiles, cannot be read (cut short, or written by a newer Slate), that launch changes nothing from it: no profile is connected again, no kept original is removed, the file stays as it is with a copy beside it ( .corrupt ), and Disconnect of a profile that shares its files with another (Cursor) is refused until the file is fixed or removed. Asking the tool first. Whether the plugin is installed, and where from, is asked of the tool's own list command when it has one: claude plugin list --json , codex plugin list --json and gemini extensions list -o json . Slate reads the tool's files only when the command is missing, fails, or does not name the plugin, and writes a warning to slate.log when one of those files is not in a form it reads. Connect re-registers a slate MCP entry that is already there when the tool's config file holds one; the tool's error text is not read. What actually ran. The MCP server records tool, account and Slate when a tool starts it. The tool's dialog shows what its last session ran: this Slate and when; one started before this Slate was built (the next session runs this one); or another Slate install, named (also on the row, behind an amber dot). A dev checkout's server run from its source counts as this Slate. The HTTP entry always reaches the running Slate; a host's stdio entry keeps the server it started with. h: Personal, and the ones you share
How a shared workspace stays in step
x: A workspace is one SQLite file on your machine holding its own docs, memory, activity, artifacts and search. Switch into one and the whole app is in it. Every workspace starts private; share one and everything in it belongs to its members (nothing is marked per doc). Personal, and the ones you share # Personal is the starting workspace and the only one that fills by itself: captured sessions, git repositories with no project doc, cross-project notes. It cannot be left or removed. Any workspace, Personal included, can be shared: Click its row in Settings → Workspaces . Use its Sharing switch. Agree to the count shown: docs, memories, activity rows and artifacts to publish. Switching off withdraws them (they were readable in between). Sharing needs the Team plan (coming soon); all else is free, including any number of private workspaces. On Free the switch is refused with a message saying so. Accounts that already shared keep sharing free until Team ships. Turning sharing off is always allowed. The switcher is at the top of the rail: Slate's mark, grey on the rail; in the open switcher each workspace's mark wears its own colour, beside its name. Shared = small people mark, failed sync = warning, read-only = padlock. Open rows say Shared or Private . ⌘\` next workspace, ⌘~ previous; with only Personal, nothing. Switching back restores the same doc, tab strip and rail section. A workspace not yet opened in this window opens on Home. Nothing carries over. What follows a switch # Per workspace: open tabs, favourites, recents, expanded sections, what Home is scoped to, automations (they belong to a group or project doc). What you were still typing when you switched, a title or a doc's text, is saved in the workspace you left. The same everywhere, kept in machine.db : theme, sidebar and rail widths, running AI sessions, the CLI accounts your tools use. Using it # Sign in : Settings → Account , GitHub. Make, share, rename, recolour, leave, remove : Settings → Workspaces (a private one renames at once; inviting needs it shared; Personal keeps its name; a workspace you belong to but have not set up here shows Add here ). Switch : the switcher, whose last row Manage workspaces… opens Settings → Workspaces. Move a doc in : right-click or ⋯, Move to ‹workspace› ( sharing ). Others' docs sit in your tree with their avatar, read-only. Ask your AI : recall with scope: "workspaces" and get_doc search and read every workspace you belong to, including ones not set up here; recall without that scope stays in the working directory's workspace. How a shared workspace stays in step # Sync runs every 2 minutes and at startup. Sync now (Settings → Workspaces) runs it at once and reports what moved. After a failure the retry waits 2, 4, 8… minutes up to 1 hour; a success resets. With no shared workspace it does nothing. Only changed rows are sent (hash of exactly the published fields); nothing new costs one query. The same comparison withdraws : a row the cloud holds that your replica lacks (in Trash, removed for good, moved to another workspace) is tombstoned upstream and every member's copy goes on their next pull. A store's first pass (new Mac, reinstall) withdraws nothing and pulls your rows down first. After that, a Mac withdraws only a row it once held: something you wrote on your other Mac since this one last synced is not in its replica yet, and arrives instead of being withdrawn. A doc you moved to Trash on one Mac is not published again by your other Mac. The withdrawal records which Mac wrote it, and your other Mac moves just that doc to its own Trash on its next sync (a doc inside it that you moved elsewhere stays). It does this once per withdrawal: if you then restore the doc from the Trash on that Mac, it stays restored and is published again. Memories and artifacts follow the same rule. A withdrawal that names no Mac (from Stop sharing, or older than this rule) is sent again after you turn sharing on again, or when you restore a doc that this Mac had already seen gone; a doc restored before that Mac's first sync after the update is not sent until then. A sync pass checks again, right before each write, that the workspace is still shared, so pressing Stop sharing while a pass runs cannot put the work back. Offline works: you are the only writer of your rows, so queue order does not matter. What actually leaves your machine # Everything in a shared workspace is for its members, except what is specific to your machine: Sent Not sent Doc title, block content and plain text for the cloud index, as written. A captured AI session's doc is never sent The rest of properties (typed and captured metadata, including a project's folder path) doc_type , parent link, your timestamps, the doc's branch label (a branch name, from properties ) position , the sibling order Memories anchored to a doc in the workspace: sentence, kind, subject, confidence, a lesson's trigger, the doc learned on A memory's reasoning body and source reference. Also never: a memory hidden from sessions, a global memory (no doc), one Slate no longer believes, one an app saved Git activity: commits and branch events with branch, commit subject (never the rest of the message) and normalised git remote (so a teammate's checkout at another path matches) A commit message body, the activity payload (file paths, diff stats, counts) and activity.repo , the absolute path Artifacts: title, kind, description, agent, the doc made under, newest version Older versions That a session happened, with branch and time Everything else: transcript, tool, session id, summary Your display name, email, avatar from the sign-in provider Anything in a workspace you have not shared Postgres enforces the activity kind list with a CHECK constraint, not the client. The right column withholds fields, not words. A doc body and a memory's sentence go up as written; a path typed in a doc or recorded by an agent in a decision goes up with the row. h: Read-only, and why there is no merge
Finding a teammate's memory from your checkout
x: Everything in a shared workspace is the team's; there is no "publish this doc" button. Keep work private in a workspace you have not shared. A doc you create there is shared at once, as is a decision your AI records, and a commit in a git repository the workspace owns lands in its activity feed. A captured AI session's doc is never published, and neither is a plan captured from a session in plan mode: it stays on this Mac. Sharing needs Team (coming soon); accounts that already shared keep it free until Team ships. Getting existing work in # Groups and projects are moved, not copied. Right-click in the sidebar or use ⋯ in the header, Move to ‹workspace› ; Slate first says how many docs move and who can read them. Moving out works the same. Whole subtree : a group takes its projects; a project takes its branches and their plans and designs. Ids kept : a published doc keeps its cloud rows. Properties come : the folder path routes the git repository to the workspace. Memory comes : memories anchored to the moved docs. A move refuses to carry one anchored to no doc. Lands at top level ; its old parent stays behind. Refuses what is not yours : a subtree with anyone else's docs, memory or activity, or a move where either workspace is read-only for you. Nothing is copied or removed. Order is read, write, remove. No transaction spans two SQLite files, so a failure between write and remove leaves the docs in both workspaces; re-run. One folder, one workspace. A folder decides where the work done in it goes, so it belongs to one workspace on your Mac. Adding a folder that another workspace already holds is refused, and the message names that workspace: move the project instead. If two workspaces still both have a project on the same folder, the one holding it keeps it, and Personal always wins, so the work stays private. Read-only, and why there is no merge # Each doc has one writer, its author. A teammate's doc opens with a read-only editor and a line giving the reason: Reason Meaning Another author A teammate wrote it (named). Their edits reach you; yours would not reach them Workspace is read-only Removed upstream, or you were removed. Everything stays readable and exportable With one writer per row there are no version columns, 409 handling or conflict resolution. Your manual sibling order is not published; on a teammate's machine your docs arrive in pull order. You on two Macs. Each Mac remembers the version of your doc it last saw in the workspace. When your other Mac published a newer version, this one takes it, and never sends its older copy over it. If you edited the same doc on both Macs before either synced, the later edit wins (by when you made it, not when it reached the cloud) and the other is kept beside it as "‹title› (copy from this Mac)". Docs, memories and artifacts all work this way. One exception: a doc or memory whose published copy has words of a hidden memory blanked out is not taken, so the words this Mac holds are never replaced; it stays as it is until you edit it here. Who wrote what (shared workspaces only): Sidebar: a teammate's doc shows their picture at the row end; yours show none. Under the title: "Written by you" or "Written by Sam". Memory: a teammate's shows their name where yours shows "you". Names come from member profiles, kept locally and refreshed at app start and when you open Members in Settings, so docs stay signed offline. An unlooked-up member shows as "A teammate". Removals travel as tombstones # A removal is a tombstone : a row saying "gone", and when. When a teammate's doc is removed, the pull re-parents your surviving children to the workspace root first; Sync now reports that count as reparented . A tombstone removes only its author's row: Trashing your doc leaves a teammate's doc under it; deleting yours forever moves theirs, with everything under it, up to your doc's parent. Memory # A memory (decision, fact , preference or state saved by remember ) is anchored to a doc; if that doc is in a shared workspace, the memory is the workspace's. What travels: What actually leaves your machine . Superseding a decision withdraws the old one on the next pass. Artifacts # An artifact published in a shared workspace belongs to it and every member sees it in Artifacts . Only you can publish a new version, rename or delete it forever; a teammate's shows who wrote it and its menu offers only Copy and Open in browser. Only the newest version travels; members keep versions they received. Removal withdraws it from everyone on the next sync. Finding a teammate's memory from your checkout # You and a colleague clone one git repository to different folders, and their memories hang on docs recording a path missing on your machine. So Slate identifies a git repository by its git remote , normalised to host/owner/repo ; when recall finds no stored path for your checkout it finds the doc recording the same remote. Only the remote counts; a checkout with no fetchable remote gets nothing. Never by name: two unrelated git repositories called site share nothing. Any clone form: git@github.com:Acme/Site.git and https://github.com/acme/site are one git repository (key lower-cased, credentials stripped). See also: Workspaces , Workspaces & Invites , Privacy & Security .

Your system browser opens. After approval the provider returns to a loopback address on Slate's local server, which does the code exchange: no code, token or password passes through the UI. The session is in cloud-session.json , a 0600 file in the app-data folder, never in a database, so exporting a workspace cannot hand over a refresh token. The address is stored lower-cased and trimmed, database-enforced, so it matches a login. It matches only an address the sign-in provider confirmed; Google and GitHub confirm it when the account is made. Pending invitations are listed with members and can be revoked before claimed. Accepting sets up the replica and the workspace appears in the switcher. A declined invitation stays declined until re-invited. The only way into a workspace is an invitation the person accepts; the database refuses an admin who tries to add someone directly, to a workspace or to its account. Telling them. Each pending row has: Action Does Email Opens your mail app with the invitation addressed and written; you send it Copy Copies the same message for Slack, Teams or elsewhere The message names the workspace and inviter, links to where Slate installs from, and states the exact address the invitation is tied to (membership is claimed by email, so another account would find nothing). Creating a workspace, and deleting one forever # New workspace (Settings → Workspaces): name, colour, whether to share. Create workspace . Sharing starts on and needs sign-in; off, it is a local file, shareable later. A shared one belongs to your account, you are first member, its replica is set up on creation. Sync now sits beside it and reports what moved; results show as a status note under the buttons. Colour is used for its mark in the switcher's list and in its settings, always beside its name. Nine, in the order new workspaces get them: Cobalt, Lagoon, Iris, Silver, Orchid, Fjord, Heather, Wisteria, Graphite. The rail's tabs and the Sessions screen wear Slate's own green, not a workspace's colour. Stored on your machine, not the shared row: everyone keeps their own and anyone can recolour whatever their role. Delete workspace forever ( General in the workspace dialog) removes every doc everyone put there, for every member, without notice; authors keep what they moved back out. Only a workspace owner or the account's owner; asks twice; nothing for anyone else. Press ⌘K anywhere. One input runs a command, jumps to a doc, or searches your workspace: doc titles and bodies, tasks, memories, reports, artifacts and captured AI sessions ( Session Capture ). What ⌘K lists # With nothing typed: Open tabs , Live sessions , Recent , Favorites , then five places under Quick navigation . Loose command matches come last, under More actions . Files come from the open workspace's projects only. When git does not answer for a checkout (a large checkout read cold, past the 5 s limit), the palette names that checkout under the results instead of showing No matches ; the other checkouts still answer, and a checkout read before keeps its last file list. A file hit is the matching line with file and line number, grouped by checkout and branch; Enter opens the file read-only at that line. The query starts at three characters. At most 200 lines are found, and the palette shows the first 30. A checkout git could not search is named under the results, as in ⌘K. Sessions in ⌘K # Every live AI session on the machine is a row. Enter opens it as a chip in the Sessions tab strip: the live terminal where Slate can attach or branch, the transcript where it cannot. On a doc that stands for a folder, Start a session here launches on the project's default tool. Second session here , Continue in a copy , Stop and the resume command are on the session's own header. It accepts a full address ( https://example.com/docs ), a local server with port ( localhost:3000 ), a bare domain ( example.com , opened over https) and the full path to an HTML file ( /srv/site/index.html ). h: Every place, one of three kinds
x: Slate runs an MCP server that gives every agent one workspace and one long-term memory: what one tool saves, the next recalls. All 16 agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Antigravity, OpenCode, Gemini, Cline, Grok Build, Kiro, Qwen Code, Droid, Hermes Agent, Goose, Kilo Code and Auggie) can connect. Connect is measured on 15 and unverified on Kiro ( Features by Agent ). What it is # Agents reach it over streamable HTTP on the running app, http://127.0.0.1:47366/mcp (the port follows the Mac user: 47366 for the first account, then 47367 and up), with the app's private key in a header; sessions start no processes. h: What an agent cannot do over MCP
x: Rules for every call in the Tool Reference . Read them when a call is refused or reaches the wrong workspace. Which workspace a call reaches # One session, one workspace. The first call with a cwd ties the session to that folder's workspace; later calls without cwd run there. If that folder is later added to a project in another workspace, or taken out of one, the session follows it to the folder's new workspace. A cwd that names a different folder in another workspace is refused with wrong_workspace and the session's workspace name: start a session in that workspace's folder instead. A folder matches its project however it is spelled: through a symlink, with .. , or by its real path. Before the first cwd , a call without one gets Personal. Only live_sessions crosses workspaces on this machine; recall with scope: "workspaces" and get_doc on a shared doc read the cloud, where Row Level Security decides. An agent run's agent reaches its task by the task's token, or from inside the task's folder, wherever the task lives. No tool is marked as reaching outside Slate. Secrets # Slate replaces recognised keys, tokens and passwords with [secret] in what an agent writes through remember , create_doc , append_to_doc , log_mission_progress , update_my_task and the summary of report_agent_run_step . It does not do this for publish_artifact and publish_widget (they carry code) or the body of report_agent_run_step . What an agent cannot do over MCP # A tool can save a typed doc and append to a doc. It cannot create a plain doc, rename, move, duplicate, trash or find-and-replace, because those are undoable gestures in Slate and MCP has no undo. An agent's MCP writes can be undone when the inverse is exact: a new doc goes to Trash, a new memory is retired. Resolving a target # get_doc and append_to_doc take a target instead of an id: Field Meaning kind branch for the branch overview, knowledge_doc for a typed child under it. cwd Your working directory. It anchors to the project, and to its active branch when branch is omitted. branch The branch to scope to. doc_type The knowledge doc's type, such as plan , design , bug-report . title The doc title, when doc_type is not enough. Slate writes only when the target resolves to exactly one doc. An ambiguous target is refused. Two tool surfaces # Operations are exposed over MCP (your agents) and in-process (Home's commands). The lists differ on purpose: slate_capabilities means nothing in-process, and Home keeps a few finer tools ( recent_activity , search_content , …). packages/shared/src/tools/operations.ts declares each concept once with its surfaces.

A curated command routes a request straight to one of Slate's own workspace tools (create a doc, search notes, ask a shared workspace) without the model choosing, so a small model works. The pipeline # Copy request → keyword routing → resolve the tool → prefill known args → model fills the rest (structured output) → one tool call "Create a plan about retries" resolves to create_doc with doc_type set; the model supplies only the title. The model returns JSON for the missing fields only, and the app merges it with the arguments it injected. A read tool runs at once. A write asks first, except under Auto-edit and Full auto, where only Create an automation and Run an automation still ask ( Approvals ). What matches # A command that writes (doc, project, agent, memory) matches only when your message opens like it ("new project for…", "draft a plan…", "remember that…", after an optional "please" or "can you"). "What's new in this project" is never a command. Anything unmatched goes to the agent's own CLI, which loops over its own MCP tools. A turn is one Slate tool call or a CLI handoff. Both halves of memory # Home reads this workspace's memory ( recall_memory ) and what colleagues wrote in every workspace you belong to, even ones this machine has not materialised ( recall_workspaces , then workspace_doc ). Your own agents reach the same two over MCP as recall with scope: "workspaces" and get_doc . Questions like "what does the team know about retries" or "has anyone solved this before" reach the shared half; "what do I know about…" stays local. A shared answer names its author. Naming a workspace routes to the shared tools, scoped to it, with no MCP connection needed ("what data do I have in my Apollo workspace"). The name counts only beside a team word ( workspace , team , shared ), so "fix the Apollo timeout bug" stays ordinary. The same abilities over MCP # Home's commands are Slate's in-app tools. Your own agents get Slate's abilities through its MCP server instead, place by place: the Tool Reference lists them, and packages/catalog/src/en/mcpCoverage.json says which tools each part of Slate serves, or why one stays in the app (ADR 0127). Run an automation is run_automation there; Create an automation has no MCP tool. See also: Home , Connected MCP Tools , Agents & Model Providers .

Sharing does nothing until you switch a workspace to shared. This guide says what then leaves, what never does, and how to take it back. Other exceptions: Privacy & Security . Rules # While no workspace is shared, sync costs one local query, no network calls, and does not renew your sign-in. A shared workspace is a separate SQLite file. A store you never shared has no cloud counterpart, so nothing in it can leak. Personal starts unshared. It holds your projects and the sessions and memories captured in them; a session in a folder no project holds is not recorded. Personal can be shared on the Team plan. The switch counts what it would publish before you agree. The rail always shows the workspace you are in. What a shared workspace sends # Assume everything is shared: docs, memories, git activity, a record that a session happened (branch and time), and artifacts. Withheld Detail Machine-specific The properties bag with a project's folder path (only a doc's branch label, a branch name, goes); the absolute path on a commit (the normalised git remote goes instead); per-file path lists from a filesystem watch or .git/index ; your local sibling ordering Content Transcript content; the reasoning body behind a memory Never sent The doc of a captured AI session; a memory that belongs to no doc (global); a memory you hid from sessions; a memory a widget saved Full list: Workspaces . Postgres enforces activity kinds with a CHECK constraint. Text is not filtered. A doc body and a memory sentence go up as written, so a path you typed travels with the row. Exception: Slate replaces keys, tokens and passwords it recognises with [secret] in every memory before storing it, and in docs an agent writes. A doc you type yourself is not checked, and neither is an artifact or widget an agent publishes ( publish_artifact , publish_widget ): they carry code. Artifacts and widgets # Live artifact. A tool-published live artifact asks the Slate window for docs, memories and sessions of its own project, read-only. Its policy blocks every connection, image, form and window to any address, and WebRTC, frames and resource hints are removed. One route remains: a script from cdnjs, jsDelivr or unpkg, whose host sees the address the doc asks for. A teammate's live artifact never reads your store. See Artifacts . Widget. A widget runs with no origin and no network (no requests, images, fonts, scripts, WebRTC, resource hints or frames) and reads what its tab shows. A write needs a permission you granted once; a memory or doc write shows its words each time before saving. A memory a widget saves is held until you release it and is never shared with a team. What a widget wrote reaches an agent quoted as data. Its data stays on this computer, and a teammate's widget never reads your store. Permission What it allows Limits github.read Read-only GitHub reads with your own gh sign-in, from four fixed kinds of address; the widget never sees the token 12 a minute MCP read A tool you allowed for that widget and ticked read-only. Pinned to its definition (a changed tool asks again); arguments checked against its schema; only servers of the widget's own workspace. The widget never sees an address, token or the server's error words 20 a minute per server github.act Only ask to approve, request changes on, comment on or label a pull request in your own lists, with words you type yourself. A card names the account that will act, every time; writes go through a fixed list of four GitHub addresses; each action is written down 5 an hour per widget, 20 for all widgets Every release tests the no-network claim in the built Slate app: a hostile widget tries every way out, and listeners on the release Mac must hear nothing. See Widgets . Who can see and write # One author per doc , enforced in the database and at local write paths. Teammates read, never modify. Postgres decides who sees what. Row Level Security is the whole access boundary; a non-member gets an empty result. An isolation test suite must pass before anything built on it ships. Your machine keeps your teammates' names. To verify their docs offline, each shared workspace's member list (display name, email, picture link) is stored in machine.db , only for people you already share with. Leaving removes it; an export does not carry it. Switching off and erasing # Switch off: Settings → Workspaces → the workspace's Sharing switch. It asks, stops publishing and withdraws what was published; your store is untouched. Cloud rows are blanked and every member's copy drops them at the next sync. Switching on again republishes. Move out: moving a doc back to Personal takes it off the server at the next pass. Erase my work tombstones every row you authored there (blanked, final). Members' copies drop them at the next sync, and sharing again does not bring them back. This is the Article 17 request. It needs you to be an editor or the owner: a viewer or a former member is told so, and nothing is reported as erased. If any row is still shared afterwards, Slate says how many. Protections around Slate's local server, the files it writes and your databases, and what it does not do. To report a vulnerability, see Privacy & Security . Contents # Keys and tool configs The local server Workspace isolation Encryption and the webview Writes, backups and restore Managed Macs Keys and tool configs # No API keys. Model providers are the agent CLIs (any of the 16) you already signed in to. Nothing is written into another tool's config until you connect one. Most tools: Slate edits the tool's MCP config and, where the tool takes hooks, installs recall hooks beside it. Claude Code and Codex: Slate runs the tool's own plugin install, then removes its own MCP entry once the plugin supplies the server, so nothing is listed twice. Connect one tool yourself, from setup's Connect step or Connect → Agents . Then Slate keeps tools you install later registered too. Launch auto-connect never reaches Claude Desktop: it gets Slate when you turn Claude Code on and keeps it when you turn Claude Code off. Until you connect a tool, auto-connect is off and no file outside Slate's data directory is touched. Turning it off removes what Slate put there and stays off across restarts. Every write copies the original aside first. Slate keeps the five newest copies of each file it rewrote and sweeps the rest at launch. Only its own go: a ‹file›.bak or ‹file›.bak-20260101-120000 you made stays. Sign-in never touches the renderer. Cloud sign-in opens your system browser and returns to a loopback address on Slate's server, which does the code exchange. No code, token or password passes through the UI. The session lands in a 0600 file outside the database. The local server # The workspace port only answers the app. The server listens on loopback. A web page you visit can POST to a localhost port (CORS only stops it reading the reply), so the server refuses any request whose Origin is not Slate's webview and any request to a non-loopback hostname (DNS rebinding). Origin proves nothing about a non-browser program, so every request also presents a token minted each run into a 0600 file ( slate-server-token ) in the app-data folder, never in a folder you moved the workspace to. The app window gets it from Slate; another process only by reading that file, which only your user can. Three cases carry no header: a CORS preflight from the app window (runs nothing), the live event stream (cannot set headers, so the token is in its address), and the two sign-in redirect landings (cloud account, work gateway). Each acts only on a sign-in Slate started, once. The auto-capture port is authenticated. With auto-capture on, a loopback port lets git hooks and shell scripts push a note into Memory. The server rejects requests that do not look like local tooling (which stops a browser), and anything that writes must present the server token (which stops other processes, since only your account reads the file). Captured notes are ranked by recall and can reach later AI sessions, hence the guard. To drive it yourself, send the token as an x-slate-token header, read from slate-server-token . One port and one token per machine. Validated tool arguments. Every MCP argument is checked against a Zod schema first. A wrong or missing type is rejected, nothing is coerced, an undeclared argument is dropped. Workspace isolation # Each workspace stays in its own file and Slate refuses to mix them. A server request must name its workspace; one that does not is refused, not filed into Personal. Slate's own code cannot open a workspace file without naming it. An agent session works in the workspace of the first folder it names and is refused another workspace's folder. Each file records its workspace, so a misplaced file does not open as another workspace. Sessions shows every workspace at once, and so does the live_sessions tool: an agent in any workspace sees every running session, with its title, last reply, goal and folder. recall with scope: "workspaces" , and get_doc on a doc shared with you, read the cloud copy of every workspace you belong to. Nothing else crosses workspaces. A test plants a marker in one workspace and asks every part of the server and every agent read for it from another. It must never come back. Encryption and the webview # Slate encrypts nothing at rest. workspace.db , shared workspace files, machine.db and their WAL sidecars are unencrypted. Confidentiality rests on your OS's full-disk encryption (FileVault, BitLocker, LUKS) and file permissions. There is no SQLCipher build, key or passphrase. Anyone with the decrypted volume and your user's read access can read every workspace. If you need application-level encryption at rest, Slate does not meet that today. The cloud session and work gateway sign-in files are unencrypted too, but 0600 and outside every database. Webview CSP. The Tauri webview runs under an enforced Content Security Policy, so the renderer cannot reach arbitrary network origins. Writes, backups and restore # Transactions. Every change is a SQLite transaction; WAL mode lets reads continue during writes. Backups. Slate copies a database aside before any schema migration and keeps the last three per store. Leaving or deleting a workspace forever also keeps a copy. Restore. Settings → Workspaces → (the workspace) → Storage → Restore a backup lists them. It applies at the next launch, and the workspace it replaces is kept too. If a connected agent still has the workspace open, the restore is refused; quit those tools and retry. Managed Macs # For IT teams that deploy Slate with an MDM (Jamf, Kandji, Intune and others). Start at login is a managed preference. Push a configuration profile for the domain app.slate.workspace with the key StartAtLogin , a boolean. true starts Slate at login on every Mac and false keeps it off. Slate reads the key only when the profile forces it. The switch in Automations › Built-in then shows your answer, says Managed by your organization and cannot be changed, and

What the export does not contain
x: Everything (docs, captured sessions, memories, decisions, automations, settings) lives in SQLite files on your machine: workspace.db (Personal), one per shared workspace, and machine.db (this computer). There is no proprietary container and no cloud copy unless you share a workspace or join one. Sharing publishes what is in that workspace, except what Workspace Sharing, Precisely says is never sent. Where the file lives # Platform Path macOS ~/Library/Application Support/app.slate.workspace/workspace.db Linux $XDG_DATA_HOME/app.slate.workspace/ ( ~/.local/share/ when unset) Windows %APPDATA%\app.slate.workspace\ To keep Personal elsewhere (an external drive or another folder on this computer), move it in Settings → Workspaces → (the workspace) → Storage . If the drive is not connected, or the file that records where Personal went cannot be read (empty after a power cut, for example), nothing opens a different empty workspace in its place: the app shows its missing-workspace screen (also when the drive goes away while Slate is open), hooks skip quietly and agents are told the workspace is not connected. If the folder is there but macOS will not let Slate open it (Documents or Desktop with access turned off in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Files and Folders), the screen says so and names that setting instead, with no Start empty here : the workspace is most likely still there, and agents are told the same.
