The same screen opens the folder. The format is open # Open workspace.db in any SQLite browser: Table Holds page The universal unit: docs, documents, mission docs, captured sessions memory Persistent knowledge with status and text routine Automations: what runs on a schedule or on an event, with its steps artifact , artifact_version Published docs and widgets, with every version task , task_step Agent runs and their steps task The lines on your Tasks list setting Workspace settings activity Commits, branch events and session records captured for this workspace audit The append-only log of workspace events Doc bodies are block JSON, and Slate converts docs to and from Markdown. Durability # WAL mode. Reads continue while the server writes. Pre-migration backup. Slate backs up the database before any schema migration. A way back from an update. The backups sit in a backups/ folder next to the workspace file, named like workspace-pre-v170.db . Slate keeps the last three per workspace. To go back to an older version of Slate, restore one in Settings → Workspaces → (the workspace) → Storage → Restore a backup , then install the older version. Without that, an older version refuses to open a workspace a newer one has changed, and says so. No backup, nothing lost. If Slate cannot write the backup (a full disk, for example), it holds back any update step that could lose data. It tells you, and finishes the update at the next launch that can make the backup. Stray workspace files are moved, never removed. At startup Slate moves an empty workspaces/‹id›.db that belongs to no workspace you joined into backups/ , only when it holds nothing beyond a brand-new database. Any other file stays. The file is standard SQLite at a known path, so you can back it up, move it or read it years from now with other tools. What the export does not contain # Your cloud session sits outside the database, in a 0600 file in the app-data folder that stays there when you move Personal, so an export never carries a live refresh token. Everything else is in the file. Before you share an export, know that: A shared workspace's export contains your teammates' work too. Sync pulls their docs, memories, activity and artifacts into your copy. Moving a doc into a shared workspace is a move, not a copy. It leaves your Personal file. A project's memory settings travel with it. They, and where you said a memory goes, are in the same file. See also # Privacy & Security Workspaces

Licensing # Free for individuals. Team plans are coming. The Free plan is everything Slate does on this Mac, with no card, no time limit, no licence key and no trial timer. Team is for shared workspaces. It has no price yet. Settings → Account shows who is signed in and your plan. On the Team card, Tell me when it's ready records that you want it, and we email you when it is. Slate is proprietary software, licensed under the Terms of Use . Your workspace stays yours on every plan: it is a SQLite file on your machine, and you can always open and export it. Auto-updates # Tauri's updater asks Slate's update service (the update Edge Function in its Supabase project) first, then the release manifest on GitHub Releases . A check sends app version, system, CPU, channel (release or prerelease) and a random install id. Files always come from GitHub Releases. Releases roll out in steps. The service can offer a release to part of the copies first and stop offering a bad one; a stopped version already downloaded is not installed on quit. The install id places your copy in a group ( Privacy ). A prerelease build also gets the next prerelease; a release build gets releases only. Slate checks 8 seconds after opening, then every 4 hours, downloads in the background and tells you when ready. On a Mac, updates usually download only what changed : a patch from the previous version, about 5% of the full download (6 MB instead of 126 MB from 0.1.53 to 0.1.54). Slate rebuilds the new version from the patch and a kept copy of the current one (about 50 MB in its cache folder), installing only if the result is exactly the published release and its signature checks out; otherwise it downloads the whole version. If macOS clears the kept copy, the next update is full. With Automatic updates on, the update installs when you next quit , never while you work or by restarting itself. With it off, a quit installs nothing and asks the update service nothing: a downloaded update waits for Restart now . Restart now in the notice first says how many CLI sessions are open. Quit and Restart now treat sessions alike: a Claude Code session goes to the background (Slate types /bg and it keeps running as a background job), a session from another tool is ended, and a session already in the background keeps running. About in Settings shows your version, any waiting update with full release notes, and Check now . A failed check or install says why, with Try again . Website, Documentation and Source lines open in your browser. If Slate won't start # After three launches in a row fail to reach a working window, the next starts in safe mode : the server runs, and the rest of the background is skipped (startup repairs, task and automation schedulers, sync, auto-capture, reminders, keep-awake, agent reconnect). One screen checks for an update at once and installs it. It says "No newer version is published yet." when there is none, "Could not check for updates" on failure, and with Automatic updates off keeps showing "Looking for a newer version…". Your workspace file is never touched. Start normally retries a normal launch; Open logs shows the log folder. See also # Platform & Availability Privacy & Security

Slate is a native macOS app: Tauri 2, a Rust host and a React 19 webview. Linux and Windows are early builds . Each Mac CPU has its own app (Apple Silicon, Intel). An installed universal copy (releases up to 0.1.54) updates to its own CPU's app. Each release also builds a Linux .deb and a Windows installer on GitHub's runners, attached only when the build passes. The early builds boot and pass tests but are not used day to day, and the Windows port is unfinished (issue #138). Platform support today # Platform Can you download it? Status macOS, Apple Silicon Yes — the curl installer Primary platform, smoke-tested macOS, Intel Yes — the curl installer Its own app, built on the release Mac for Intel. Before each release it boots, and its sidecar builds an app, through Rosetta Linux (x86_64, .deb ) Not in the latest release (0.1.69) A release attaches it only when it builds, installs and boots on Ubuntu 22.04 Windows 10/11 Not in the latest release (0.1.69) Being ported; a release attaches the installer only when its Windows build passes Slate needs macOS 13.5 (Ventura) or later (bundled server: Node 24). LSMinimumSystemVersion in Info.plist makes an older Mac refuse to open the app rather than show a window with no server. For Linux, each release's platform build runs the Rust tests on a GitHub Ubuntu 22.04 runner, builds the .deb , installs it and waits up to 60 seconds for the app to log that it started. On Linux: shortcuts read Ctrl instead of ⌘ closing the window minimizes it the tray icon has a menu (Open Slate, Quit Slate), because a Linux tray reports no clicks Slate watches a project and your agents' transcript folders one folder at a time, never inside node_modules , caches or .git . A folder named like build output ( dist , build , out , target , venv , vendor ) is skipped too, unless git tracks a file in it: then it is source and its edits show in Activity. It uses at most a quarter of fs.inotify.max_user_watches , and no more than 8,192. At the cap it says so once in its log and stops adding folders. Git and the periodic checks still see changes there. Releases are cut by hand on an Apple Silicon Mac, which also builds the Intel app and signs the Linux .deb and the Windows installer with the same updater key. How you install it # Run the curl command in Getting Started . It downloads the prebuilt app, checks checksum and code signature, and installs to /Applications ; a missing or wrong checksum, or a signature other than Slate's own certificate, stops it. There is no Homebrew cask, App Store listing or AppImage. A .deb or Windows installer comes from the GitHub release when it carries one (the site's README says which). Each release also carries one .dmg per CPU ( Slate_‹version›_aarch64.dmg , Slate_‹version›_x64.dmg ). It is not the supported path. Slate is signed with its own self-signed certificate and is not notarized by Apple, and macOS quarantines whatever a browser downloads, so the image opens with "Apple could not verify Slate is free of malware". On macOS 15 and later only System Settings → Privacy & Security clears that. curl sets no quarantine flag, which is why the installer is a script. How you remove it # Run the curl command in Uninstalling : it removes Slate's entries from agents and the app, and keeps your workspace unless you ask otherwise. x: When nothing changes, Slate does nothing. If you are not typing, no file changed and no AI session is writing, Slate uses almost no CPU and wakes your Mac as little as it can. Slate's tests measure this against the limits below, and a change that goes over one fails them. Limits only go down. When a change makes Slate cheaper, its limit drops in the same change. The limits # Each number is the most Slate may use. Each limit was set from the median of several measured runs, plus room for a busy machine: twice the measured CPU, 10% more memory, size and wake-ups. The tables are written from the limits file the tests read, so this guide cannot disagree with them. MB is 1,024 × 1,024 bytes. ‹!-- footprint:end --› How they are measured # The tests use no data of yours. They make their own stores and launch their own copy of the app. Five parts: The server. It runs on three made-up stores built from a fixed seed: a new user, six months of use and a heavy user. The test starts the server, lets it settle, then watches it for a fixed time while nothing happens. It records CPU, how often the server woke to run code, and memory at the end, as Activity Monitor shows it (memory written to, not memory macOS can take back). The server while AI sessions work. The six-months store, with two made-up AI sessions in a made-up home folder, one in a project folder and one in a plain folder, one writing every 2 seconds. The test records CPU and counts every program the server starts on its own (such as git ), through stand-ins that log each start. While only the sessions' own writing changes, that count must be zero. Your real sessions are never read. The server in use. The heavy store with 600 MB of made-up AI sessions captured (three still running), and Tasks, Sessions and Memory opened. Two minutes after launch the test reads the memory the server's code still holds after everything unused is cleared. The app. A test copy opens each screen in turn and stays on it, idle. The test adds the CPU of every process the copy owns: the app, its server and the web view helpers macOS starts. Then it hides the window and measures once more. The size. The download ( .dmg ), the installed app ( .app ), and the part of the app and server built for each chip. A number over its limit is measured again, and counts only if both runs are over, so a short spike on a busy machine does not fail a change. The limits come from one Mac, named under the tables. A slower Mac may show a higher percentage for the same idle Slate. Check it yourself # Use Activity Monitor (Applications → Utilities). Leave Slate open on any screen and do not touch it for a minute. In the CPU tab, search for Slate . You see the app and its server ( slate-mcp ). Add their % CPU . The tables also count the web view helpers, so the real total is a little higher. In the Energy tab, read Slate's Energy Impact and Avg Energy Impact . An idle Slate sits near zero. A high average while you did not use it is worth reporting. Hide the window (⌘H) and look again. That is the "Window hidden" row. Your numbers can exceed the idle limits for a good reason. While an AI session writes, Slate reads it as it happens, which is work you asked for. The "while AI sessions work" limit covers that. Slate reads what a session wrote and starts no programs on a timer to check on it. A working session does not keep the screen moving. Its dot on the rail and in Sessions moves when the session starts working or starts waiting on you, then holds still. Slate's tests reject any animation that never ends, except while something finishes on its own, such as a web page loading or an app being built. It should be reviewed and completed by qualified counsel before any commercial release, and jurisdiction, contact, and licensing details filled in. Slate is a local-first desktop application. It is built so that your workspace lives on your machine and nothing leaves it without an explicit action on your part. This policy explains what Slate stores, where it stores it, and the narrow set of cases where data crosses the boundary of your device. The short version: you sign in once with Google or GitHub, your account holds your name, email and plan, your workspace is a file you own, and the only workspace content that ever reaches a server is what is in a workspace you specifically choose to share. Your Account # Slate requires an account. On first launch you sign in with Google or GitHub. Sign-in is handled by Supabase Auth, in Slate's own Supabase project. The account holds: your name, email address and picture link, as supplied by Google or GitHub; which of the two providers you signed in with; your plan (Free, or Team when it is available); if you asked to hear when Team is ready, that you asked and from which screen. The account holds none of your docs, sessions or memories. The sign-in session is kept in a permission-restricted file ( cloud-session.json ) in Slate's application-data folder, never inside a database, so later launches work offline. When you are online, Slate contacts its Supabase project at each start and whenever the sign-in token renews. It renews the token, makes sure your account exists, and reads which workspaces you belong to. Those requests carry your account id and your IP address, and no workspace content. Supabase Auth also keeps sign-in logs that hold your IP address. Invitations. When you invite someone to a shared workspace, their email address and the role you chose are stored in our database until they accept or decline. Slate sends no email: the invitation opens in your own mail app, and you send it. What Slate Stores, and Where # Everything you create in Slate — docs, the block-editor content, agent runs, captured AI sessions, decisions, memories, automations, skills, and settings — is stored locally in SQLite database files on your device: workspace.db for your Personal workspace, one more file for each shared workspace, and machine.db for the settings that describe this computer. Slate stores no embeddings and downloads no machine-learning model. Memory is retrieved by keyword matching computed on your device, re-ordered by word statistics that Slate fits in memory from your own stored memories and never writes to disk or sends anywhere. Item Location Workspace database See per-platform paths below Sign-in session A permission-restricted file ( cloud-session.json ) in Slate's application-data folder, never inside a database The workspace database lives at: Copy macOS ~/Library/Application Support/app.slate.workspace/workspace.db Linux $XDG_DATA_HOME/app.slate.workspace/ Windows %APPDATA%\app.slate.workspace\ You can override the location with the SLATE_DB_PATH environment variable. The database uses WAL mode, and Slate takes an automatic backup before running schema migrations. Slate holds no provider API keys. Where Slate drives a command-line tool (see below), that tool holds its own authentication under its own configuration. Your Slate sign-in session token is written to a permission-restricted file in Slate's application-data folder rather than inside any database, so exporting your workspace cannot hand anyone a live credential. What Leaves Your Device, and When # Slate's default posture is that nothing leaves the machine. Apart from your sign-in (above), four standing exceptions run without a click each time. Three of them need your choice or your opt-in first. The update check runs by default, and you can switch it off. A problem report you send, requests you start yourself and connections you set up are described after the four. Model calls made by your own installed CLIs. Slate's model providers (called "agents") drive command-line tools you have already installed and authenticated — the agents you connect (16 supported, see the docs ). When you use Home, a session, an agent run or an automation, the relevant CLI sends your prompt and context to that provider to generate a response, when you ask it to or on a schedule you set. A cloud session sends your project's code to the vendor's computer (Claude Code clones the project's GitHub remote, or uploads the code if there is none). On my phone connects a session to claude.ai, and Anthropic keeps that conversation. Slate does not hold a raw provider API key; the CLI makes the request under its own account and its own terms. What is sent, and to whom, is governed by the provider you chose (see "Third-Party Model Providers" below). The contents of a shared workspace you create or join. Slate includes an optional team layer. Sharing a workspace needs the Team plan. Every workspace is unshared until you choose to share it, and a workspace that has never been shared has no counterpart in our database at all — nothing about it is transmitted, and nothing can be. Your Personal workspace begins unshared. Choosing to share it shows you a count of what would be published before you confirm. Within a shared workspace, the rows you author are copied to a hosted Postgres database (Supabase) where that workspace's members can read them.
